papers.title: Modern cell-based assays for biomedical research: from conventional methods to AI-driven high content analysis.
papers.abstract: In vitro cell-based assays are fundamental tools in biomedical research, supporting investigations of cellular physiology, disease mechanisms, drug discovery, toxicology, regenerative medicine, and precision therapeutics. However, conventional two-dimensional (2D) cell culture models often fail to recapitulate the structural complexity and physiological functions of native tissues, prompting the development of advanced platforms, including three-dimensional (3D) cultures, organoids, organ-on-a-chip technologies, and microphysiological systems. Recent advances in cell viability and cytotoxicity assessment, functional cellular analysis, molecular profiling, clustered regularly interspaced short palindromic repeats (CRISPR)-based functional genomics, high-content imaging, flow cytometry, single-cell and spatial multi-omics, and automated high-throughput screening have expanded the analytical capabilities of cell-based assays. Furthermore, the integration of artificial intelligence (AI)-assisted image analysis and computational biology has enhanced cellular phenotyping, biomarker discovery, and mechanistic investigation, with the potential to improve the prediction of therapeutic efficacy and toxicity. Nevertheless, challenges related to physiological relevance, technical variability, inadequate standardization, high operational costs, scalability, poor reproducibility, cell-line misidentification, batch-to-batch variation, and inconsistent reporting continue to hinder translational applications. Future progress will depend on integrating physiologically relevant models with AI-driven analytics, spatial multi-omics, digital pathology, automated screening, and microphysiological systems. Standardized protocols, harmonized reporting practices, and interdisciplinary collaboration will be essential to improve reproducibility, strengthen regulatory acceptance, advance precision medicine, and reduce reliance on animal experimentation. In this context, this review critically evaluates conventional and emerging in vitro cell-based assays, emphasizing their biological principles, analytical capabilities, translational applications, and practical limitations, while highlighting future opportunities to improve predictive accuracy, reproducibility, and clinical translation.

papers.title: LUNA-FM: a subword foundation model for long non-coding RNAs for functional inference.
papers.abstract: RNA foundation models (FMs) have shown promise for RNA identification and functional annotation. However, many use single-nucleotide tokenization, which produces long input sequences and can increase computational costs when modelling long RNAs, including long non-coding RNAs (lncRNAs). To address these limitations, we introduce LUNA-FM (Length-efficient sUbword-based Nucleic Acid Foundation Model), an RNA language model pretrained on approximately 28 million redundancy-filtered ncRNA sequences. LUNA-FM combines subword tokenization with a long context transformer, enabling efficient modelling of long RNA transcripts. We systematically evaluate tokenization strategies and vocabulary sizes to investigate the trade-offs between sequence compression, representation granularity, computational efficiency, and downstream performance. Across multiple RNA prediction tasks, including transcript classification, subcellular localization, and RNA-protein interaction prediction, LUNA-FM achieved competitive performance compared with existing RNA FMs while reducing effective input length and fine-tuning cost. We also found that frequency-based subword tokenization generally produced more stable and effective representations than likelihood-based approaches, although the optimal vocabulary size remained task dependent. Training-set motif discovery identified candidate motifs enriched relative to matched low-attribution and dinucleotide-shuffled controls of preeclampsia-associated lncRNAs. Overall, our findings highlight the task-dependent effects of subword tokenization and vocabulary size, extend RNA FM evaluation to longer transcript inputs, and establish LUNA-FM as a competitive model with favourable recorded fine-tuning times.

papers.title: From Viral Detection to Disease Measurement: Lessons from COVID-19.
papers.abstract: The COVID-19 pandemic demonstrated a fundamental distinction between detecting an infectious stimulus and measuring the disease produced by that stimulus. SARS-CoV-2 establishes infection, whereas COVID-19 reflects the interaction among viral replication, host immunity, inflammation, endothelial dysfunction, coagulation and tissue injury. These processes are related but are not interchangeable measurements. A positive molecular test establishes evidence of viral genetic material; it does not, by itself, quantify tissue injury, systemic thromboinflammation or disease severity. Similarly, individual biomarkers measure components of a biological response rather than necessarily defining the complete disease state. Clinical outcomes, including hospitalization and death, provide important measures of consequence but do not necessarily identify the mechanisms that produced them. COVID-19 therefore provides a case study in measurement fidelity: the quantity measured must be distinguished from the biological process that the investigator seeks to understand. Viral evolution, changing population immunity, vaccination, immune imprinting and human behaviour further demonstrate that the relationship between infection and disease changes over time. Future pandemic preparedness should integrate pathogen detection with mechanistically appropriate measurements of host response, tissue injury and clinical outcome, while maintaining explicit boundaries between measurement, inference and causation.

papers.title: Artificial Intelligence in Screening and Early Detection of Prostate Cancer.
papers.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) is transforming prostate cancer screening and early detection through the integration of clinical-risk calculators, magnetic resonance imaging (MRI), digital pathology, genomics, biomarkers, and liquid biopsies. AI-enhanced risk models may improve biopsy decisions, while AI-assisted MRI interpretation can increase the detection of clinically significant disease and reduce false positives, unnecessary biopsies, and overdiagnosis. Digital pathology algorithms may support more reproducible tumor identification, Gleason grading, and prognostic stratification. Genomic risk scores, kallikrein-based tests, and emerging circulating biomarkers further enable precision screening by identifying men at elevated risk and refining the selection for imaging or biopsy. However, most available systems address isolated components of the diagnostic pathway, and evidence from prospective, real-world screening populations remains limited. Clinical implementation therefore requires external validation, screening-specific calibration, implemented reference standards, and workflow integration. Ultimately, multimodal AI may enable a "virtual biopsy" that combines imaging, molecular, pathological, and clinical data to deliver personalized, noninvasive prostate cancer assessment.

papers.title: Global biogeography and regional abundance-occurrence patterns of potential pathogenic bacteria in nearshore waters.
papers.abstract: Nearshore waters receive terrestrial inputs and support intensive human activities, yet the global distribution and ecological organization of potential pathogenic bacteria in these waters remain poorly understood. This study harmonized 1,158 seawater 16S rRNA gene amplicon samples from 15 ecogeographic regions. Potential pathogenic taxa were detected in 387 samples (33.4%) across 13 regions, with regional detection prevalence ranging from 0 to 85.7% (permutation chi-square test, P < 0.001). Proteobacteria and Firmicutes accounted for 94.4% of the potential pathogenic subset. Potential-pathogen-containing genera and overall bacterial genera showed similar positive abundance-prevalence relationships and nonlinear latitudinal patterns in genus richness. Community similarity decreased with geographic distance in both groups (Mantel r = 0.217 and 0.133, respectively; both P = 0.001). The fitted decline was shallower for potential-pathogen-containing genera, but region-cluster bootstrap and leave-one-region-out analyses showed that the slope difference was sensitive to regional composition. Overall bacterial genus composition differed among regions (PERMANOVA R 2 = 0.271, F = 29.947, P = 0.001), although dispersion also differed. After controlling for geographic distance, aquaculture-farm exposure showed the strongest positive associations shared by overall bacterial genus composition, potential-pathogen-containing genus composition and potential pathogenic species composition (partial Mantel r = 0.303, 0.261 and 0.352, respectively; all FDR q < 0.01). Species-level models identified contrasting associations of detection with salinity, chlorophyll a and neighbourhood exposure proxies. These results establish a global ecological baseline for interpreting potential pathogenic bacterial signals and designing regionally targeted nearshore surveillance.

papers.title: Establishment of a RAA-CRISPR/Cas12a system-based nucleic acid detection method for avian reticuloendotheliosis virus.
papers.abstract: Reticuloendotheliosis virus (REV) is an immunosuppressive and oncogenic pathogen that causes substantial economic losses in poultry production. In the absence of commercial vaccines and specific therapeutic agents against REV, early and accurate detection is essential for REV control and eradication. In this study, a visual RAA-CRISPR/Cas12a assay was established for REV detection based on a conserved 552-bp region of the pol gene. RAA primers and crRNA were screened, and the reaction conditions were systematically optimized. The assay was completed at 37 °C with 20min of RAA amplification and 40min of Cas12a reaction, and results were read visually under blue/UV light. The limit of detection was 10 copies/μL. The assay showed no cross-reactivity with other common avian pathogens and exhibited good repeatability. When 90 clinical samples were tested, the RAA-CRISPR/Cas12a assay detected 50 positive samples (55.55%), whereas qPCR detected 43 positive samples (47.77%). The overall agreement was 85.56% (77/90), with a positive agreement of 93.02% (40/43), a negative agreement of 78.72% (37/47), and a Cohen's kappa of 0.713. These results indicate that the RAA-CRISPR/Cas12a assay is a rapid, specific, and visual method for REV detection and provides a complementary tool for REV screening, although further validation with live birds and other sample types is required.

papers.title: The Role of Diagnostic Tools in the Management of Ventilator Associated Lower Respiratory Tract Infections.
papers.abstract: Ventilator-associated pneumonia (VAP) remains a leading healthcare-associated infection in intensive care units and is closely associated with prolonged mechanical ventilation, excessive antimicrobial exposure, higher costs, and poor clinical outcomes. Despite decades of clinical trials and guideline development, bedside diagnosis remains limited by the absence of a biological reference standard. Conventional criteria combine nonspecific clinical, radiographic, and microbiological findings and cannot reliably distinguish parenchymal infection from airway colonization, endotracheal tube biofilm, or sterile pulmonary inflammation. Syndromic multiplex polymerase chain reaction panels, metagenomic next-generation sequencing, and host response profiling have greatly increased analytical sensitivity and shortened the time to microbiological information. They have also exposed the amount of microbial and inflammatory noise present in the ventilated airway. Detection of an organism, a resistance determinant, or systemic inflammation does not by itself establish causality. This review examines the strengths and limitations of clinical scores, imaging, respiratory sampling, conventional culture, rapid molecular assays, antimicrobial resistance testing, systemic and alveolar biomarkers, host transcriptomics, breath analysis, and artificial intelligence-based models. It proposes that VAP should be approached as a time-updated probability of tissue invasive infection rather than a binary diagnosis. A practical host-pathogen attribution framework should integrate the timing and trajectory of respiratory deterioration, specimen quality, relative pathogen burden and dominance, resistance and virulence signals, local and systemic host responses, prior antimicrobial exposure, and competing diagnoses. Diagnostic tests should be ordered only when a predefined management decision is linked to the result, followed by structured reassessment at 48 to 72 hours. This approach may improve antimicrobial targeting while reducing treatment of colonization and other noninfectious mimics.

papers.title: Environmental suitability and high-risk hotspots of Leptospira spp. in southern Chile.
papers.abstract: Leptospirosis is a zoonotic disease caused by bacteria of the genus Leptospira, widely distributed and of high importance to both public and animal health. In Chile, available studies have mostly focused on pathogen detection, leaving a limited understanding of the environmental factors that determine its distribution. Ecological niche modeling offers a powerful approach to address this gap by identifying the environmental conditions associated with pathogen presence. In this context, we propose a large-scale spatial analysis of the Los Ríos and Los Lagos regions using a maximum entropy algorithm to predict areas suitable for Leptospira occurrence and to identify the key environmental drivers shaping its distribution. We integrated occurrence data of Leptospira spp. in wildlife and livestock with environmental variables: Normalized Difference Vegetation Index (NDVI), land surface temperature, precipitation, wetness index, and land-use components, derived from principal component analysis. This approach enabled the identification of key environmental factors and to map areas of high environmental suitability for Leptospira spp. We developed two risk maps: (i) a continuous map of environmental suitability for Leptospira spp., and (ii) a binary map delineating areas of high transmission risk based on an ecological suitability threshold. The variables with the greatest contributions were NDVI and tree cover (the latter analyzed within a principal component). Areas within the central valley and the margins of water bodies showed higher environmental suitability for the pathogen. These findings highlight priority areas where strengthened epidemiological surveillance is warranted.

papers.title: A novel 17-plex multi-pathogen detection for rapid and accurate diagnosis of tick-borne diseases.
papers.abstract: In recent years, anthropogenic ecological disruption has escalated tick-borne zoonoses; ticks transmit taxonomically diverse pathogens with overlapping clinical signs, challenging precise diagnosis and increasing risk of simultaneous detection in pooled samples. Despite advancements, current sequencing technologies, such as Next-Generation Sequencing (NGS), Polymerase Chain Reaction (PCR) assays, and antibody-based detection methods, are hampered by limitations including extended processing times and limited detection throughput. These constraints significantly hinder their effectiveness in high-throughput pathogen screening for animal or patient samples. To address these challenges, we developed an innovative multi-detection method based on the Multi-analyte Suspension Assay (MASA), enabling rapid and accurate diagnosis of a comprehensive panel of 17 vector-borne pathogens. This 17-plex panel comprises Rickettsia spp., Anaplasma phagocytophilum, Borrelia recurrentis, Babesia spp., Borrelia burgdorferi, Rickettsia prowazekii, Rickettsia heilongjiangensis, Orientia tsutsugamushi, Coxiella burnetii, Leptospira, Bartonella spp., Candidatus Ehrlichia erytraense, Hantaan Virus (HTNV), Seoul Virus (SEOV), Crimean-Congo Hemorrhagic Fever Virus (CCHFV), Severe Fever with Thrombocytopenia Syndrome Virus (SFTSV), and Tick-Borne Encephalitis Virus (TBEV). By combining this novel method with traditional techniques, including nested PCR and Real-Time Quantitative Reverse Transcription PCR (qRT-PCR), we achieved accurate detection of pathogens such as Rickettsia spp., Anaplasma phagocytophilum, and SFTSV in tick samples. Notably, the technique revealed the co-existence of multiple pathogens within the same sample group, highlighting its ability in identifying co-detection of pathogens. Additionally, in suspected cases of tick-borne pathogen infection in febrile patients, the method quickly identified positive results for SFTSV and Rickettsia spp. These preliminary results suggest the potential of this method as a promising screening tool for clinical diagnostics, although larger-scale validation is warranted. This method provides a preliminary technical candidate approach for the development of more sensitive field-deployable detection tools.

papers.title: Reconsider the diagnosis of community-acquired pneumonia: A case report of tracheobronchial tuberculosis.
papers.abstract: Mycoplasma pneumoniae is transmitted through respiratory droplets, with an incubation period of 1 to 3 weeks. This bacterium is globally endemic, with infections peaking in summer and early fall. Pulmonary tuberculosis (TB) poses a major global health issue, often requiring computed tomography for detection of subtle lesions. Targeted treatment for single-pathogen infections usually shows significant improvement within about a week, but the rise of mixed infections complicates clinical management. A 25-year-old male presented with a 2-month duration of intermittent cough and 3 days of shortness of breath and fever. Lab results showed a slightly elevated white blood cell count, neutrophil percentage, and C-reactive protein. An anti-M pneumoniae immunoglobulin M test was positive, suggesting M pneumoniae infection and serving as the basis for the initial diagnosis of community-acquired pneumonia. The patient was subsequently treated with levofloxacin. However, his condition worsened, leading to bronchoscopy, which revealed a positive sputum acid-fast bacilli smear and Mycobacterium tuberculosis polymerase chain reaction. He was subsequently diagnosed with tracheobronchial TB. The patient received empirical levofloxacin for 5 days. Because his symptoms worsened, bronchoscopy was performed, and after a positive acid-fast bacilli smear and M tuberculosis polymerase chain reaction, standard anti-TB therapy with isoniazid, rifampin, ethambutol, and pyrazinamide was started. Cough improved transiently on levofloxacin but recurred with paroxysmal exacerbations and night sweats. After anti-TB therapy, cough and fever resolved, and follow-up computed tomography 6 months later showed marked resolution of the bronchial luminal narrowing and deformity. Radiologic manifestations of tracheobronchial TB vary with host factors, and diagnosis involves multiple pathological considerations, especially if other organisms are present alongside M tuberculosis.

papers.title: SH3TC2-Charcot-Marie-Tooth type 4 C: an Italian multicentre cohort study.
papers.abstract: Charcot-Marie-Tooth disease type 4 C (CMT4C), caused by biallelic variants in SH3TC2, is the most common autosomal recessive demyelinating neuropathy. Italian multicentre data with detailed genotype-phenotype characterisation are lacking. Yet knowledge of the natural history is urgently needed as SH3TC2 gene replacement therapy approaches clinical trials following a successful Pre-Investigational New Drug meeting with the FDA in November 2024. We screened 684 patients with genetically unresolved CMT using a combination of exome analysis and a multigene next-generation sequencing panel and identified nine (from five Italian neurology centres) with biallelic SH3TC2 variants. All patients underwent standardised neurological examination, nerve conduction studies, and assessment using the Charcot-Marie-Tooth Examination Score version 2 (CMTESv2). Variant pathogenicity was assessed according to American College of Medical Genetics and Genomics and Association for Molecular Pathology (ACMG/AMP) criteria incorporating REVEL (Rare Exome Variant Ensemble Learner) and CADD (Combined Annotation-Dependent Depletion) scores. Nine patients (5 males, 4 females; age 3.5-66 years) were studied. Twelve distinct SH3TC2 variants were identified, including four not previously reported: p.Glu794* (likely pathogenic according to ACMG/AMP guidelines), p.Gly18Ser (variant of unknown significance, VUS), p.Ala526Thr (VUS), and p.Thr1098Ile (VUS). Scoliosis was present in 6/9 patients (66.7%), foot deformities in 7/9 (77.8%), and sensorineural hearing loss in 2/9 (22.2%). Genotype-phenotype analysis revealed marked intra-class variability, including a 59-year-old with homozygous frameshift variants and near-normal function (CMTESv2 total score of 3). One patient was diagnosed presymptomatically at age 3.5 years through cascade genetic testing prompted by comorbid features of Angelman syndrome. All seven symptomatic patients showed motor nerve conduction velocities below 35 m/s. Novel variants p.Gly18Ser and p.Ala526Thr are of uncertain significance and require functional validation: p.Ala526Thr lies immediately adjacent to the functionally characterised pathogenic residue Arg529, whereas p.Gly18Ser lies 16 residues from the myristoylation site at Gly2, within a segment of very low predicted model confidence. This Italian multicentre cohort expands the SH3TC2 mutational spectrum highlighting the marked phenotypic variability of CMT4C, and the possibility of presymptomatic identification through multigene NGS panels. Our data contribute to the evidence base required for the design of forthcoming gene therapy clinical trials.

papers.title: RNAcomp2D: a web tool to execute multiple methods and visually compare predictions of RNA secondary structure.
papers.abstract: Ribonucleic acids (RNAs) are involved in many important biological processes. In particular, non-coding RNAs are crucial regulators of cellular processes, playing a significant role in gene expression. RNA secondary structure is key to infer their specific function and for understanding how they interact with other molecules. Many computational models have been developed in the last decade to predict the secondary structure, achieving increasingly higher success rates. However, each new method has its own input-output interface, programming language, computational requirements and, sometimes, a dedicated server to run the model or just a source code in a repository. Thus, nowadays it is very hard to obtain predictions from multiple methods and compare them at once. A unified interface is urgently needed, which allows accessing several methods at the same time, visualizing and comparing predictions among them, and also with a reference structure when available. We introduce here RNAcomp2D, a web-based tool that allows users to enter an RNA sequence, or select one from RNAcentral, and obtain predictions of RNA secondary structures using several state-of-the-art methods. Both classical thermodynamic methods and the latest deep learning models are packaged in containers and accessible in an unified website. All the predictions, and the reference structure if available, are shown at the same time in a single graphical interface. Moreover, as new models continue to be developed, this tool is designed to be scalable, allowing the addition of more prediction methods in the future. Web server is available at https://sinc.unl.edu.ar/web-demo/rnacomp2d/. Data and source code are available at https://github.com/sinc-lab/RNAcomp2D. Supplementary data are available at Bioinformatics online.

papers.title: A Hybrid Large Language Model and Diffusion Framework for Rational Promoter Design.
papers.abstract: High-performance promoters are essential tools for precisely regulating gene expression, yet their rational design within the vast combinatorial sequence space remains a major challenge. Here, we present a hybrid framework that integrates a large language model (LLM) with a diffusion model to enable data-driven and interpretable promoter design. The fine-tuned LLM predicts promoter strength with high accuracy and, through systematic sequence mutations, identifies biologically essential core regions. A diffusion model is then conditioned on these core regions to reconstruct non-core regions and generate complete promoter sequences. We experimentally validated this approach in Escherichia coli by high-throughput barcoded promoter activity sequencing: 7.78% of the designed promoters outperformed the benchmark promoter BBa_J23119, with the best variants reaching approximately 2.5-fold the expression level of BBa_J23119. By explicitly coupling interpretability with generative design, this strategy provides a practical framework for promoter design in E. coli and may be adaptable to other regulatory sequence engineering tasks.

papers.title: Investigation of Parkinsonism-Associated Genes in a Large Cohort of Individuals with Early-Onset or Familial Predominant Parkinsonism.
papers.abstract: A study of a large cohort, including early-onset or familial patients with Parkinson's disease (PD), has deciphered the contribution of known PD genes. However, many other genes, thereafter labeled parkinsonism-associated genes (PAG), are associated with other neurological conditions in which parkinsonism is sometimes reported. The aim was to evaluate the contribution of these genes in patients with predominant parkinsonism. We performed whole-exome sequencing in a cohort of 1488 probands with early-onset (here defined by an age at onset <45) or familial predominant parkinsonism (1756 in total) who did not have a pathogenic variant in seven known PD genes (GBA1, LRRK2, PARK7, PINK1, PRKN, SNCA, VPS35). One hundred eighteen PAGs were selected for the analysis based on their assessment by experts in three different consortia (Genomics England PanelApp, PanelApp Australia, International Genetic Nomenclature in Movement Disorders Study Group). Pathogenic variants were extracted from these genes according to the criteria of the American College of Medical Genetics. Eighty-one probands (5.4%) carried a pathogenic variant of one PAG. Clinical review (available for 71/81 probands) revealed that the phenotype was compatible with the variant in 91.5% (65/71) of probands. Thirty-seven genes were considered disease causing. Among them, six (ATP13A2, ATXN2, FIG4, GCH1, PLA2G6, PPP2R5D) accounted for a large proportion of probands with a compatible phenotype (26/65, 40.0%). Our results indicate that PAGs would account for about 5% of patients with early-onset or familial predominant parkinsonism not mutated for known PD genes, and that clinical evaluation is essential to establish causality. © 2026 The Author(s). papers.title: On-Column RNA Preservation Enables Cold-Chain-Free Virome Analysis of Chili Peppers.
papers.abstract: High-throughput sequencing (HTS) has become an essential tool for plant virus surveillance and discovery, but its application in field settings is often limited by the need to preserve high-quality RNA under cold-chain conditions. This challenge is particularly acute for chili pepper ( Capsicum spp.), which has strong endogenous RNA-degrading activities. To address this limitation, we developed an on-column RNA-preservation workflow that enables cold-chain-free transport of extracted RNA for virome analysis. Laboratory preservation tests showed that RNA extracted using conventional methods degraded rapidly during ambient-temperature storage, whereas RNA that was retained and dehydrated directly on a silica column remained stable. The workflow was validated using RNA extracted from symptomatic chili pepper samples collected in Indonesia. RNA remained highly intact after extraction in a laboratory and subsequent 3-day transport at ambient temperature. Using HTS of the preserved RNA, we identified a diverse virome, including near-complete genome sequences of Capsicum annuum amalgavirus 1, pepper cryptic virus 2, and chili veinal mottle virus as well as begomovirus- and polerovirus-related sequences. These detection results agreed with RT-PCR assays for individual RNA viruses and PCR assays for DNA viruses. These findings demonstrate that on-column RNA preservation enables reliable, cold-chain-free transport of extracted RNA for virome analysis and provides a practical framework for plant virus surveillance and molecular diagnostics in regions where cold-chain infrastructure is limited.

papers.title: Optimization of a Lab-screening Procedure to Evaluate Seed Treatment Efficacy: Detection of Ustilago nuda in Hordeum vulgare Seedlings.
papers.abstract: To prevent plant disease outbreaks and economic losses, rapid and reliable tools to evaluate newly developed, low-risk treatments are needed. Visual inspections of grown plants are used to assess treatment efficacy a labor-intensive and costly process, especially for seedborne pathogens that are asymptomatic until flowering. For one such pathogen, Ustilago nuda that causes loose smut of barley ( Hordeum vulgare ), we developed a lab-screening procedure combining optimized growth procedures and qPCR to quantify its DNA in seedlings, thereby accelerating seed treatment evaluations. We cultivated seedlings for 5, 10 and 14 days with two techniques: growth on filter paper in dark and in potting soil under light-dark conditions. Seedlings were grown from two naturally infected seed lots, which were either not treated or treated with a synthetic fungicide or warm water. During two seasons, these non-treated and treated seeds were also grown in the field. Infection levels in the seedlings were based on qPCR-measured U. nuda DNA normalized to H. vulgare DNA. Treatment efficacies were calculated using laboratory-measured infection levels and field-observed disease incidence, and a lab-to-field predictability factor was used to compare seed treatment evaluations among the seedling growth procedures. Infection levels assessed using qPCR on seedlings grown for 10 days on filter paper and 14 days in potting soil most accurately represented field results and showed clear treatment effects. Our lab-screening method could provide an early and efficient evaluation of seed treatment efficacy, aiding in the development of new, low-risk control strategies to reduce synthetic plant protection product applications.

papers.title: FusionGDB 3.0: integrating breakpoints, generating personalized sequences, and inferring tumorigenic scenarios for human fusion genes.
papers.abstract: FusionGDB has served diverse biological, health, and clinical research communities as a unique functional annotation knowledgebase of human fusion genes. In this study, we report an updated resource of human fusion gene annotation (FusionGDB 3.0), available at https://compbio.uth.edu/FusionGDB/. FusionGDB 3.0 includes substantial content updates: 156K up-to-date human fusion genes established by integrating 216K RNA-seq-based and 100K WGS-based breakpoint events, comprehensive open reading frame annotations, protein domain retention searches, and 1.13 million personalized fusion protein sequences reflecting individual nsSNVs from TCGA and CCLE, as well as N- and C-truncated protein sequences alongside canonical in-frame products. Furthermore, it incorporates 18K potential tumorigenic scenarios, supported by evidence from the literature, spanning drug-targetable gene group fusions, the epigenomic architecture around breakpoint junctions, and therapeutic prioritization scoring. FusionGDB 3.0 establishes a systematic framework for the functional annotation of coding structural variants. FusionGDB 3.0 serves as a pivotal reference knowledgebase for the genomics, oncology, and precision pharmacology communities, while also functioning as a foundational benchmark dataset for training and validating machine learning models, structural biology platforms, and AI-driven therapeutic discovery pipelines.

papers.title: An integrative single-cell long noncoding RNA atlas reveals regulatory programs in the pan-cancer tumor microenvironment.
papers.abstract: Long noncoding RNAs (lncRNAs) have been shown as critical components in cancer genomics, yet their functionality and regulation remain elusive. Here, we present an integrative lncRNA atlas covering more than 370,000 cells from 18 cancer types. In addition to multiple lineage- and cellular state transition-associated lncRNAs, we identify a set of lncRNAs that are embedded within cell type-specific regulons, suggesting associations between lncRNA expression and cell type-enriched transcriptional programs. By integrating CRISPR-based functional genomic screens and clinical data, we further prioritize not only CRISPR-supported candidate lncRNAs linked to tumor cell fitness and immune cell state features but also specific lncRNA signatures correlated with patient survival and immunotherapy response.

papers.title: GenNA: Conditional generation of nucleotide sequences guided by natural language annotations.
papers.abstract: Deciphering the mapping between biomolecular sequences and complex biological functions is a central challenge in genomics. While existing generative nucleotide models capture sequence distributions, they lack explicit access to gene-associated biological semantics, limiting semantics-guided design. Here, we present GenNA, a generative nucleotide foundation model guided by natural language annotations. Pretrained on a multimodal nucleotide-text corpus spanning 2221 eukaryotic species (∼416 billion characters), GenNA internalizes relationships between sequence syntax and functional semantics within a unified autoregressive framework. Without explicit rule-based supervision, GenNA yields distinguishable perplexity responses to sequence-annotation mismatches, mutational variants, and species-label perturbations. Furthermore, across diverse generation tasks, GenNA produces statistically plausible nucleotide sequences consistent with target semantics, structural constraints, and species contexts. Overall, GenNA provides a versatile framework for controllable nucleotide generation, establishing a practical route to integrate functional descriptions with sequence design.

papers.title: Exploratory single-cell multiomics suggests naive CD4 + T cell dysregulation in treatment refractory rheumatoid arthritis.
papers.abstract: Around 20% of patients with rheumatoid arthritis (RA) have disease that remains refractory to multiple targeted treatments, highlighting a major clinical challenge. We determine single-nucleus transcriptional and chromatin landscapes (10x Genomics Epi Multiome) on 14,625 primary CD4 + T-cells isolated from treatment-naive early and refractory (defined as per the EULAR definition of difficult-to-treat) patients with RA. We systematically analyze circulating regulatory profiles to reveal potential mechanisms and therapeutic targets that may contribute to the difficult-to-treat phenotype. We highlight disease-stage-specific alterations in naive and Th1-like memory CD4 + T-cells. In particular, refractory naive cells show signatures of heightened activation, upregulation of pathways aligning with T cell anergy, diminished regulation at regulatory loci (e.g., FOXP1, ICOS) and blunted stimulation responses; consistent with a more desensitized or exhausted state. Genes such as LGALS3, ZBTB7B and FOXO4 emerge as potential candidate regulators of the difficult-to-treat state. Finally, through RA GWAS integration, we prioritize putative causal variants in cis-regulatory elements.

papers.title: Toll-like receptor 4-driven translational reprogramming in macrophages is unaffected by Salmonella SPI-1 activity.
papers.abstract: Changes in gene expression during bacterial infection are the combined result of altered transcription and translation, with the latter comparatively understudied. Gram-negative bacteria rapidly trigger cytokine gene transcription in macrophages through the activation of pathogen-associated molecular pattern receptors, for example the detection of Salmonella lipopolysaccharide (LPS) from the bacterial cell envelope by Toll-like receptor 4 (TLR4). Here, through time-resolved parallel translatomic and transcriptomic profiling, we now show temporal TLR4-specific translational upregulation of cell signaling proteins in macrophages induced by Salmonella . While transcriptional upregulation of these genes is dampened through the activity of the Salmonella SPI-1 type 3 secretion system, a robust translational response remains. These data reveal an important host-pathogen translational regulatory network that modifies the innate immune response of macrophages to infection.

papers.title: Standing genetic variation facilitates climatic adaptation in the invasive grapevine pathogen Plasmopara viticola under demographic bottlenecks.
papers.abstract: Invasive pathogens often experience demographic bottlenecks during colonization, yet how they rapidly adapt remains unclear. Plasmopara viticola , the causal agent of grapevine downy mildew, provides a model to address this question. Using β-tubulin sequences and whole-genome data, we reconstructed its invasion history and adaptation in China. Our analyses support a North American ancestral origin of Chinese P. viticola , while demographic modeling and ABBA-BABA tests indicate historical connections between Chinese and European-related lineages, suggesting a complex invasion history. Chinese populations showed reduced genetic diversity and regional bottlenecks, with the low-latitude population showing the most pronounced reduction in effective population size. Despite these constraints, candidate adaptive variants were frequently retained as polymorphisms in other populations and occurred at relatively high frequencies, supporting an important role for selection on pre-existing genetic variation during climatic adaptation. These findings highlight how invasive pathogens can retain adaptive potential despite severe founder effects.

papers.title: Integrated experimental tools for Trypanosoma evansiisolation, diagnosis, and ultrastructural analysis.
papers.abstract: Trypanosoma evansi, the causative agent of surra, infects diverse mammals across Asia, Africa, and South America, posing significant veterinary challenges. Experimental tools for its isolation, culture, diagnosis, and ultrastructural characterization remain limited. Here, we developed an integrated methodological toolbox comprising in vivo parasite isolation using immunodeficient mice, adaptation to in vitro culture, a multi-host antibody detection ELISA, a sensitive TaqMan qPCR assay for species-specific detection, and Ultrastructural Expansion Microscopy applied directly to bloodstream parasites. This approach enabled stable parasite maintenance, accurate diagnosis, epidemiological surveillance, and detailed visualization of cell cycle dynamics, revealing the absence of kinetoplast DNA in the studied strain. Together, this toolbox provides a versatile framework to advance the study of T. evansi biology and supports improved research and surveillance efforts for this neglected veterinary pathogen.

papers.title: Microbial hazards and contamination dynamics in warm marine seafood supply chains: From detection to predictive risk management.
papers.abstract: Warm marine seafood systems face distinctive microbial safety challenges arising from elevated environmental temperatures, climate-sensitive Vibrio ecology, cold-chain vulnerability, and heterogeneous supply chains. This review critically examines how environmental drivers of indigenous marine pathogens interact with post-harvest contamination and microbial amplification from harvest to retail, and evaluates the implications for HACCP verification, microbial risk assessment (MRA), molecular surveillance, traceability, and preventive control. The evidence indicates that seafood microbial risk is cumulative and stage-dependent: environmental baseline hazards are modified by time-temperature history, water and ice quality, sanitation, handling, processing, and cross-contamination. Reliance on endpoint and predominantly qualitative microbiological sampling limits source attribution, obscures contamination and amplification points, and constrains quantitative exposure assessment. We therefore propose an integrated environment-to-consumer framework linking stage-specific quantitative microbiology with environmental monitoring, predictive microbiology, molecular source attribution, HACCP verification, traceability, and quantitative MRA. Particular emphasis is placed on pathogenic Vibrio spp. as climate-sensitive hazards and on the complementary roles of culture-based and genomic methods in determining viable hazards and contamination pathways. Oman and the Gulf Cooperation Council are considered as a regional case within the broader context of tropical and subtropical seafood systems. The central priority is a transition from endpoint pathogen detection toward longitudinal, quantitative, and predictive microbial risk management capable of identifying where hazards originate, where they are amplified, and which interventions most effectively reduce consumer exposure.

papers.title: Integrating Pan-Genomics and Machine Learning into Foodborne Pathogen Traceability.
papers.abstract: Whole-genome sequencing (WGS) has become central to the investigation of foodborne outbreaks and the surveillance of bacterial pathogens, including Salmonella enterica, Listeria monocytogenes, Campylobacter spp., and Shiga toxin-producing Escherichia coli. Routine workflows rely heavily on core-genome multilocus sequence typing (cgMLST) and reference-based single-nucleotide polymorphism (SNP) analysis. These approaches provide reproducible measures of relatedness but do not systematically represent plasmids, prophages, genomic islands, and other accessory elements that can influence antimicrobial resistance (AMR), virulence, host adaptation, and persistence. Pan-genome analysis offers a way to examine both core and accessory variation, while machine learning (ML) can use these genomic features to estimate source, phenotype, and risk. This narrative review evaluates how these approaches are being integrated into foodborne pathogen traceability. We describe the strengths and limitations of core-genome typing, review genomic feature representations and learning algorithms, and assess applications in host and geographic attribution, virulence assessment, and AMR prediction. Particular attention is given to study design, including population-structure-aware data splitting, fold-specific preprocessing, external validation, and comparisons of core-only, accessory-only, and combined feature sets. The evidence supports a complementary, dual-pathway framework rather than replacement of established typing methods: cgMLST and SNP analysis remain well suited to rapid, auditable cluster detection, whereas pan-genome-informed ML can add probabilistic predictions of biological function and risk. Progress toward routine use will depend on representative benchmarks, transparent reporting, biological interpretation, and validation in operational settings.

papers.title: Genomic surveillance reveals age-structured SARS-CoV-2 transmission across settings.
papers.abstract: Understanding respiratory virus transmission requires integrating pathogen genomic data with detailed epidemiological context. We analyzed >85,000 SARS-CoV-2 genomes linked to epidemiological data collected in Massachusetts from November 2021 to January 2023. Collected in 666 settings, including schools, colleges, and skilled nursing facilities, this dataset enabled direct comparison of within-setting transmission to community-wide risk. Elevated transmission was concentrated in specific age-defined subpopulations-older adolescents in schools, undergraduates in colleges, and residents in nursing facilities-with little additional risk among other groups, notably including staff. Young adults, particularly in colleges, played a disproportionate role in spread, and new viral lineages consistently expanded first within this group. Viral spread followed reproducible urban-to-rural gradients, and vaccination was associated with reduced onward transmission. We further estimated sequencing thresholds required for timely detection of emerging variants. Together, these findings reveal consistent demographic and spatial structure in SARS-CoV-2 transmission that can inform viral respiratory pathogen genomic surveillance.

papers.title: Applications of computer vision in mosquito-borne diseases: A systematic review.
papers.abstract: Mosquito-borne diseases (MBDs) remain a major global health challenge. Vector surveillance, pathogen detection, and clinical diagnosis are central to control efforts but are limited by labor-intensive workflows and shortages of trained personnel. Computer vision (CV) offers opportunities for scalable automation throughout the MBD management pipeline. We aimed to systematically characterize the applications of computer vision in mosquito-borne diseases research, summarize methodological developments, and identify opportunities and barriers to translating these advances into public health practice. We conducted a systematic review in accordance with PRISMA 2020 guidelines, searching PubMed, Scopus, and IEEE Xplore for studies published between January 1, 2010, and December 31, 2025, that applied computer vision to any aspect of MBD research or control. A total of 1,521 records were screened, and 650 studies met the inclusion criteria. Studies were categorized by computer vision application area, data types, algorithmic approaches, and data acquisition methods. Descriptive quantitative analysis and qualitative thematic synthesis were performed. The use of computer vision in MBD research increased significantly over the review period. Most studies focused on diagnostic applications, particularly Plasmodium detection in malaria microscopy. More recent work incorporated deep learning models for mosquito species classification, UAV- and satellite-based habitat mapping, and smartphone-based non-invasive diagnostic imaging. Emerging areas included 3D mosquito behavioral analysis and Internet of Things-enabled surveillance. Algorithmic approaches evolved from traditional image processing to convolutional neural networks, You Only Look Once (YOLO)-based object detectors, and transformer architectures. However, most models were developed using small, geographically-limited datasets, lacked external or prospective validation, and were rarely evaluated in operational settings, limiting their translational readiness.

papers.title: Gut microbiome functional genomics and PBPK modeling: a systems framework for precision therapeutics.
papers.abstract: The gut microbiome is increasingly recognized as an important determinant of interindividual variability in the disposition and response to pharmaceuticals, nutraceuticals, and dietary bioactives. Conventional microbiome profiling based primarily on taxonomic composition provides limited mechanistic insight into these effects, whereas functional genomics and multi-omics approaches enable characterization of microbial genes, enzymes, pathways, and metabolites involved in xenobiotic biotransformation. This review examines the integration of gut microbiome functional genomics with physiologically based pharmacokinetic (PBPK) modeling as a systems framework for precision therapeutics. Particular emphasis is placed on translating microbial gene-enzyme-metabolite relationships and experimentally characterized biotransformation kinetics into quantitative PBPK parameters. Metagenomics, metatranscriptomics, metaproteomics, and metabolomics provide complementary information for resolving microbial metabolic potential and activity, while genome-scale and community metabolic models can identify candidate pathways for xenobiotic transformation and metabolite production. Microbiome-aware PBPK approaches may incorporate microbial biotransformation, metabolite formation, gastrointestinal transit, absorption, and temporal functional variability. Whether these additions improve exposure predictions requires evaluation against conventional PBPK models using independent pharmacokinetic datasets.Artificial intelligence and machine learning may further support functional feature identification and hybrid PBPK modeling, provided that predictions remain biologically interpretable and experimentally validated. Despite its potential, clinical translation is constrained by limited standardized kinetic data, microbiome variability, incomplete functional annotation, and insufficient prospective validation. Integrating validated microbial functional information with mechanistic PBPK modeling may ultimately provide a quantitative basis for microbiome-informed prediction of drug and nutraceutical exposure and advance individualized therapeutic strategies.

papers.title: Plant pathogenic continuum in the microbiome era.
papers.abstract: Plant pathology has traditionally relied on a binary distinction between pathogens and non-pathogens, or between harmful and beneficial microorganisms. However, this distinction is becoming increasingly difficult to maintain in the microbiome era. For many plant-associated microorganisms, pathogenicity is not a fixed property but varies along a gradient depending on host physiology, microbial strain, environmental conditions, resident microbiota, and time. This review discusses a plant pathogenicity continuum as a framework for interpreting this fluidity. Within this continuum, we discuss four interconnected positions: true or near-deterministic pathogens, context-dependent pathogens, opportunistic pathogens, and pathobiome- or dysbiosis-associated disease states. These positions should not be treated as rigid categories, but as reference points that help compare how strongly disease depends on the host, environment and microbiome interactions. We also discuss the strain-level problem in plant pathology, because species or pathovar-level detection often does not capture real differences in virulence and host range. Finally, we consider the diagnostic implications of this continuum, especially where pathogen detection alone is not sufficient. This continuum-based view may help plant pathology move from naming pathogens toward interpreting disease states.

papers.title: Clinical Utility of Nanopore-Based Targeted and Metagenomic Sequencing for Rapid Diagnosis of Infections.
papers.abstract: Rapid diagnosis is critical for acute invasive infections, yet conventional culture is time-consuming. The real-time, long-read capability of nanopore sequencing facilitates rapid diagnosis, but standardized workflows are lacking. Here, we describe 2 nanopore sequencing workflows, nanopore targeted sequencing (NTS) and nanopore metagenomic sequencing (NMgS), for pathogen and antimicrobial resistance identification. A total of 176 residual clinical specimens, of which >90% were abdominal, pleural, joint, abscess, and bile samples, were analyzed using the NTS and NMgS workflows and compared with culture. NTS employed multiplex PCR to amplify 16S rRNA gene, internal transcribed spacer region, and 30 resistance genes, while NMgS involved host DNA depletion and unbiased sequencing. Among 152 culture-positive samples, NTS achieved 98.68% positivity, compared with 69.08% for NMgS. NTS identified 79.93% of cultured species, while NMgS detected 44.89%. For 24 culture-negative samples, NTS identified potential pathogens in 6 cases, whereas NMgS detected none. For antimicrobial resistance detection, NTS achieved a sensitivity of 84.62% for β-lactam resistance, 62.50% for quinolones, and 31.25% for aminoglycosides, with corresponding specificities of 87.10%, 75.86%, and 96.61%. Conversely, NMgS showed lower sensitivities of 36.84%, 16.67%, and 12.50% for these classes, while maintaining 100% specificity across all categories. Using the 4-h sequencing workflow, NTS and NMgS achieved comparable sample-to-report times (10.83 vs 10.41 h). This study demonstrates the potential of nanopore sequencing for rapid diagnosis and provides practical insights for its implementation in clinical laboratories. While NTS is sensitive and cost-effective, NMgS offers a hypothesis-free approach. These workflows may complement routine culture in specific clinical contexts.

papers.title: Surveillance bias and the hidden ecology of Enterovirus coxsackiepol: implications for global risk assessment of vaccine-derived poliovirus emergence.
papers.abstract: Global enterovirus (EV) surveillance has long relied on RD/L20B cell culture systems optimized for poliovirus (PV) detection. This systematically under-detected Enterovirus coxsackiepol (EV-C) while over-representing Enterovirus betacoxsackie (EV-B). This bias created a fundamental paradox: circulating vaccine-derived polioviruses (cVDPVs), including those of novel oral polio vaccine type 2 origin, have genomic regions of non-polio EV-C origin, suggesting frequent recombination with viruses rarely detected in surveillance datasets. Here, we show that EV-C viruses might be more prevalent and widely distributed than recognized. We further show that regions considered low risk for cVDPV emergence (especially those using only inactivated PV vaccine and acute flaccid paralysis surveillance) may harbor undetected non-polio EV-C circulation and silent PV transmission. We propose integrating wastewater (WW) surveillance, long-range reverse transcription-PCR (amplifying the complete or coding-complete genome as a single contig), and long-read sequencing to capture full EV diversity, improve cVDPV emergence risk assessment, and strengthen PV-eradication efforts. Expanding this framework to other viruses can facilitate the 100-day mission by enabling the acquisition of actionable intelligence for all such viruses directly from WW. Furthermore, this creates an opportunity to harmonize PV surveillance with broader pandemic preparedness frameworks, allowing investments in PV genomic surveillance to generate cross-pathogen benefits.

papers.title: Genetic variants of transthyretin amyloidosis with cardiomyopathy associated with low sensitivity to bone scintigraphy: a systematic review.
papers.abstract: Transthyretin cardiac amyloidosis (ATTR-CA) is characterized by amyloid deposition and frequently leads to a progressive cardiomyopathy with poor prognosis. Bone scintigraphy with 99m Tc-labeled tracers is the cornerstone of noninvasive diagnosis, yet several hereditary TTR variants are associated with false-negative or low-grade tracer uptake. To identify all TTR variants associated with false-negative bone scintigraphy in hereditary ATTR-CA and discuss clinical implications. Medline, Scopus, and Cochrane were searched from inception to July 2025 per PRISMA guidelines. Eligible studies included observational studies, case series, and case reports of patients with confirmed ATTR-CA undergoing TTR genetic testing and 99m Tc scintigraphy. Nineteen studies (108 patients) met inclusion criteria. Thirteen pathogenic TTR variants were associated with low or absent uptake (Perugini grade 0-1); p.Val50Met, p.Phe84Leu, and p.Ser97Tyr were most consistently implicated, while p.Val142Ile showed false-negative results in ∼5-10% of carriers. In 11 of 13 variants, advanced structural cardiomyopathy was confirmed despite negative scintigraphy. Bone scintigraphy has important limitations in specific hereditary TTR variants. A negative scan does not exclude cardiac involvement in genetically at-risk patients. Multimodal strategies including CMR and histological assessment are essential for timely diagnosis.

papers.title: GI-DB: a comprehensive variant database for exploring the extensive genetic diversity of the Indian population.
papers.abstract: The Indian population, characterized by extensive ethnolinguistic and biogeographical diversity, is significantly underrepresented in global genomic resources limiting the development of genomic medicine in South Asia. To address this, ~10 000 genomes from 83 populations were sequenced as part of the GenomeIndia initiative (Department of Biotechnology, Government of India). Here, we present GI-DB (accessible at https://ibdc.dbt.gov.in/gidb/), a public resource cataloging 136 million high-confidence variants, including 44 million variants which are not present in other global and South Asian databases. GI-DB serves as a population-specific reference resource for genetic variation across Indian populations. It can support the interpretation of clinically relevant variations for rare disease, complex disorders, and pharmacogenomics. The database is structured to provide allele frequency stratification across tribal and non-tribal groups, biogeography, and ethnolinguistic categories. The interactive browser facilitates exploration of variants and genes of interest, offering detailed annotations from tools like VEP, ClinVar, and comparisons with global databases like 1000 Genomes, gnomAD, and GenomeAsia. Researchers can search using different modalities and access data programmatically. GI-DB is a foundational resource for genomics-informed public health and clinical genetics, tailored for the Indian population.

papers.title: Molecular mechanisms and regulatory networks governing Yersinia biofilm formation and host adaptation.
papers.abstract: The genus Yersinia includes three human pathogens- Y . pestis , Y. pseudotuberculosis , and Y. enterocolitica -where biofilm formation plays distinct roles in transmission and environmental persistence. All three species share the core biofilm machinery-the hmsHFRS operon, encoding enzymes for poly-β-1,6-N-acetylglucosamine (PNAG) exopolysaccharide production, and the c-di-GMP signaling controlling this production-but their regulatory networks and biofilm outputs differ. Transcriptional control of hms involves an integrated network that includes the Rcs phosphorelay (reshaped by rcsA pseudogenization), PhoP/PhoQ, EnvZ/OmpR, BarA/UvrY, Fur/Zur, CRP-cAMP, RovM/RovA, and multiple sigma factors. Post-transcriptionally, the Hfq-sRNA and CsrA-CsrB/CsrC systems modulate gene expression; the latter is directly validated in Y. pestis and Y. pseudotuberculosis , whereas its role in Y. enterocolitica is inferred from genomic conservation. At the translational and enzymatic levels, polyamines sustain Hms protein production, while redox signals govern the HmsC-HmsD disulfide switch, controlling diguanylate cyclase activity. This multi-layer architecture ensures that biofilm output is tuned to species-specific ecological niches. In host adaptation, Y. pestis transitioned from a foodborne enteric pathogen to a flea-borne lifestyle through key genetic events-acquisition of ymt , pseudogenization of rcsA , inactivation of y2909 / y3389, and ureD -which are not shared with Y. pseudotuberculosis or Y. enterocolitica , thereby explaining their different biofilm-dependent transmission strategies. Studies in Caenorhabditis elegans have identified host O-glycosylation modifications as receptors for biofilm attachment. This review summarizes progress on the molecular mechanisms, regulatory networks, and host-adaptive functions of Yersinia biofilm formation and proposes future research directions to address knowledge gaps. Future priorities include the identification of c-di-GMP effectors, flea-specific signals, 3D biofilm imaging, and CRISPR-based detection.

papers.title: X-Linked Agammaglobulinemia Diagnosed in Adolescence Complicated by Invasive Aspergillosis: A Case Report.
papers.abstract: X-linked agammaglobulinemia (XLA) is a primary humoral immunodeficiency that is typically recognized in early childhood. We report a 16-year-old male with recurrent respiratory tract infections (RTIs) since childhood who presented with severe pulmonary infection and focal neurological deficits. Immunologic evaluation showed profound hypogammaglobulinemia, with serum IgG of 0.24 g/L and both IgA and IgM < 0.10 g/L, together with virtually absent peripheral CD19+ B cells (0.00%). Genetic testing identified a hemizygous Bruton tyrosine kinase (BTK) c.1039G > C (p.Ala347Pro) variant. Metagenomic next-generation sequencing (mNGS) of bronchoalveolar lavage fluid (BALF) detected the Aspergillus flavus/oryzae complex. Serum and cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) galactomannan (GM) tests were positive, and brain magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) revealed multiple ring-enhancing lesions. Taken together, these findings supported invasive pulmonary aspergillosis with possible central nervous system (CNS) Aspergillus involvement. This case illustrates the clinical heterogeneity of XLA, including delayed recognition until adolescence, and underscores the importance of integrating immunologic, microbiological, mycological, imaging, and longitudinal clinical evidence when interpreting multiple pathogen-detection results in complex infections.

papers.title: Atypical inflammatory bowel disease and multi-system inflammation expand the phenotype of inhibitor of nuclear factor kappa B kinase subunit beta gain-of-function variants.
papers.abstract: Gain-of-function (GoF) variants in the inhibitor of nuclear factor kappa-B kinase subunit beta (IKK2) protein, encoded by inhibitor of nuclear factor kappa B kinase subunit beta (IKBKB), have previously been reported to cause autoinflammation with a progressive immunodeficiency. Genetic defects have not previously been described in inflammatory bowel disease (IBD), although disruption of highly interacting proteins, such as IKBKG and RELA, are known causes of monogenic IBD. Using whole exome sequencing data, we screened a cohort of over 1250 adult and paediatric onset patients with IBD for deleterious variants (minor allele frequency < 0.0005, Combined Annotation Dependent Depletion [CADD] > 15) in IKBKB. We retrieved in-depth phenotypic data and performed peripheral blood mononuclear cell CD25/CD70 stimulation validation in patients with apparent IKBKB GoF variants. We identified 11 patients with potentially pathogenic variants. Correlation with clinical and immunophenotypic data prioritised a rare, potential gain-of-function, variant in a patient and his affected parent, c.522T>G, p Asp174Glu. The proband had multi-system inflammation and severe atypical inflammatory bowel disease with rectal stricturing. We demonstrated impaired CD25/CD70 T- and B-cell responses in the patient, characteristic of the IKBKB defect, alongside hallmark immunological manifestations of reduced natural killer and B-cell numbers, and perturbed immunoglobulin titres. Treatment with a selective Janus kinase (JAK1)-inhibitor resulted in rapid clinical and biochemical improvement. This study expands the phenotypic manifestation of IKBKB GoF variants to include IBD and demonstrates a biologically plausible targeted treatment. Further functional work is required to elucidate the precise mechanism of bowel inflammation and identify additional patients.

papers.title: Incidence and visual outcomes of post-intravitreal injection endophthalmitis: a single-centre analysis of 224,397 injections.
papers.abstract: Post-injection endophthalmitis (PIE) is a rare, vision-threatening complication of intravitreal injections (IVIs). As IVI volumes rise globally, optimising prevention and management is crucial. This study evaluated PIE incidence, risk factors, microbiology, and outcomes over ten years. A retrospective cohort study of 224,397 IVIs. We analysed demographics, agent type, and preparation (pre-filled syringe [PFS] vs. manual aliquoting). Overall endophthalmitis incidence was 0.029% (n = 65), and 0.026% for anti-VEGFs. PFS-ranibizumab had the lowest incidence (0.014%) and was significantly safer than manually prepared bevacizumab (0.039%; OR: 2.74 [95% CI: 1.36-5.55], p = 0.003); vial-sourced aflibercept (0.027%) was intermediate and not statistically distinguishable from either. Culture positivity was 33.8% (n = 22), predominantly Gram-positive (81.8%), with Staphylococcus epidermidis being the most common (45.5%). In univariate analysis, culture positivity was the sole predictor of worse final visual acuity (VA) (p = 0.030), though limited by small sample sizes. Median VA worsened from 0.61 logMAR at baseline to 2.10 logMAR at presentation, recovering to 1.80 logMAR at final visit (p < 0.001). Among cases initially treated with tap and intravitreal antibiotics (TAI), 60% (21/35) required subsequent vitrectomy (PPV). No baseline clinical parameters predicted TAI success or PPV requirement (all p > 0.05). Dexamethasone implants, with their larger applicator, carried the highest risk. Among anti-VEGFs, PFS ranibizumab demonstrated the most favourable safety profile, with the lowest incidence of PIE. Manual immediate-use bevacizumab aliquoting is a safe, cost-effective alternative in resource-limited settings. In univariate analysis, culture positivity emerged as a negative prognostic factor, though this finding is limited by small sample sizes. Given unpredictable TAI responses, aggressive monitoring and a low PPV threshold are essential.

papers.title: Mechanistic Insight Into ROS-Mediated Antibacterial Signaling Enables Hierarchical Hollow Polyhedral Nanozymes for Autonomous Bioelectronic Sensing and Synergetic Theranostics.
papers.abstract: Postoperative bacterial infections remain a major clinical challenge, necessitating rapid and precise diagnosis alongside effective therapeutic intervention. Herein, we report a mechanism-driven platform integrating hierarchical hollow CuSe polyhedral nanozymes for autonomous bioelectronic sensing and synergistic antibacterial therapy. Guided by first-principles calculations, the engineered CuSe nanozymes facilitate interfacial electron transfer and reactive oxygen species (ROS) generation. Integrated into an enzymatic biofuel cell (EBFC), the platform enables self-powered electrochemical and thermal dual-mode detection of Salmonella Typhimurium, achieving limits of detection (LOD) of 1.12 and 0.81 CFU mL -1 , respectively, over a linear range of 10-10 7 CFU mL -1 . Furthermore, CuSe exhibits a photothermal conversion efficiency of 45.53%, enabling enhanced ROS-mediated antibacterial activity under near-infrared (NIR) irradiation, with almost no visible bacterial colonies observed after 25 min of treatment. Transcriptomic analysis identified 88 differentially expressed genes, revealing alterations in metal ion homeostasis, oxidative stress responses, and bacterial metabolic pathways. Additionally, machine learning-assisted integration of electrochemical and thermal signals improves quantitative prediction performance compared with single-mode analysis. This study establishes an integrated strategy combining self-powered pathogen detection, synergistic antibacterial activity, and intelligent data analysis for potential point-of-care testing (POCT).

papers.title: Multiplex PCR for the Identification of the Salmonid Pathogen Tenacibaculum finnmarkense and Discrimination of the Finnmarkense and Ulcerans Genomovars.
papers.abstract: Tenacibaculum finnmarkense is an important pathogen of farmed salmon in Norway and Chile, comprising the finnmarkense and ulcerans genomovars. This study aimed to develop a multiplex PCR (mPCR) assay for species-specific identification of T. finnmarkense and discrimination between its two genomovars using comparative genomics. Comparative pan-genome analysis of 127 genomes identified genomic regions suitable for species- and genomovar-level discrimination. A gene encoding a LuxR-family protein was selected for species-level identification, generating a 313-bp amplicon. For genomovar discrimination, a gene encoding a protein of unknown function was selected for the finnmarkense genomovar, whereas a TroA-family protein-encoding gene was selected for the ulcerans genomovar, generating 659-bp and 427-bp amplicons, respectively. The assay was validated using DNA from 34 T. finnmarkense isolates and 28 non-target bacterial pathogens, with no non-specific amplification observed. Using pure bacterial suspensions, detection limits were 2.4 ± 2.83 × 10 6 CFU/mL for T. finnmarkense genomovar finnmarkense HFJ and 2.8 ± 3.5 × 10 6 CFU/mL for the ulcerans genomovar LBP5. The assay specifically identified T. finnmarkense and discriminated between its two genomovars from pure bacterial cultures. However, its relatively high detection limits and validation using pure bacterial suspensions do not support direct detection from fish tissues. The assay therefore provides a rapid molecular alternative for the identification and genomovar assignment of cultured T. finnmarkense isolates recovered from suspected cases of tenacibaculosis.

papers.title: Proteome- and phenome-wide studies identify circulating protein drivers of kidney diseases.
papers.abstract: Proteome-wide Mendelian randomization (PWMR) provides a genetic framework to identify circulating proteins causally implicated in chronic kidney disease (CKD) and prioritize them for drug discovery. However, the diverse etiologies of CKD and clinical presentations make it difficult to translate proteomic findings into actionable targets. Here, we studied protein associations with longitudinal kidney outcomes, CKD subtypes, and phenome-wide traits to identify proteins that are causally relevant and pharmacologically actionable. We performed a PWMR study using cis-pQTLs as genetic instruments for 2807 circulating proteins from four proteogenomic cohorts (ARIC, Fenland, deCODE, and UK Biobank) and tested their effects across four kidney outcomes (eGFR, incident CKD, incident kidney failure, annualized eGFR slope) in up to 464,631 of Million Veteran Program participants. Proteins meeting proteome-wide significance underwent sensitivity testing, Bayesian colocalization, and external replication in CKDGen Consortium information. The same instruments were re-tested against nine diagnosis code-defined CKD subtypes using genome wide association studies meta-analysis across the Million Veteran Program participants, UK Biobank, and FinnGen, and against 1020 phecodes to distinguish kidney-restricted from systemic effects. Druggability was evaluated using ChEMBL annotations layered onto high-confidence STRING protein-protein interaction networks. We identified 93 proteins with proteome-wide significance, and twelve remained robust across sensitivity testing (ANGPTL3, FAM213A, GCKR, GSTA1, IDI2, INHBA, INHBC, MANBA, MICB, MST1, NRG4, UMOD). Forty-seven proteins mapped to at least one of nine kidney disease subtypes, with distinct patterns across diabetic, hypertensive, and glomerular kidney diseases. Phenome-wide testing separated seven proteins with kidney-restricted associations from those with broader systemic effects. Thirty-four proteins were pharmacologic targets, nominating candidates such as IL-1 pathway blockade for diabetic kidney disease and ANGPTL3 inhibition for podocyte protection. Our integrative PWMR framework resolves circulating protein targets across CKD etiologies, separates kidney-restricted from systemic effects, and delivers actionable targets that may accelerate therapeutic innovation for CKD. About one-third of the 93 proteins could be targeted with existing or investigational medications.

papers.title: Decoding the Epigenome and Epitranscriptome by Mass Spectrometry: From Molecular Mapping to Biomarker Discovery.
papers.abstract: Epigenetic and epitranscriptomic modifications represent fundamental regulatory layers that control chromatin organization, messenger RNA (mRNA) processing, and cellular identity. Aberrant regulation of these chemical marks, including DNA and RNA methylation, hydroxymethylation, and post-translational modifications (PTMs) of chromatin-associated proteins, is strongly implicated in the development and progression of cancer, neurodegenerative, autoimmune, and metabolic disorders. Mass spectrometry (MS) has emerged as a powerful analytical platform for decoding these complex systems, offering high sensitivity, quantitative accuracy, and molecular specificity for characterizing epigenetic and epitranscriptomic landscapes. In this review, we provide a comprehensive overview of MS-based strategies for qualitatively and quantitatively mapping DNA and RNA modifications at both global and site-specific levels. Key analytical approaches, including untargeted MS workflows, isotopic labeling techniques, targeted quantification, and ion mobility spectrometry (IMS), are discussed in the context of improving detection sensitivity, accuracy, and coverage. We further highlight the integration of MS with complementary multi-omic platforms, such as genomics, transcriptomics, and metabolomics, to enable systems-level insights into chromatin regulation and RNA modification networks. Emerging technologies, including single-cell and spatially resolved MS, are also discussed for their ability to resolve cellular heterogeneity and map epigenetic alterations in complex biological systems. Finally, we examine the translational potential of MS-based epigenomic and epitranscriptomic profiling for biomarker discovery and precision medicine. Despite ongoing challenges related to sample complexity, detection of low-abundance modifications, and data interpretation, continued advances in instrumentation, informatics, and integrative workflows are positioning MS at the forefront of molecular diagnostics, bridging the gap between mechanistic insight and clinical application.

papers.title: Optimization of whole-cell human depletion provides increased sensitivity and microbial genome coverage from respiratory metagenomic assays.
papers.abstract: Metagenomics is being adopted worldwide as a laboratory-developed test. We have previously reported a unified metagenomic method for the direct detection of microorganisms from respiratory samples, delivering preliminary results within 6 h with >90% sensitivity for both viral and bacterial pathogens. This has now been deployed across the United Kingdom National Health Service (NHS) through the NHS Respiratory Metagenomics Network. Since this deployment, we have identified a number of improvements to the method to further increase sensitivity. In this manuscript, we report these optimizations, including the addition of a bead-beating cycle, substitution of the endonuclease enzyme, and controlled termination of the endonuclease reaction. This updated protocol (v1.2) resulted in substantially improved assay performance. Validation in 6 NHS hospitals using both protocols in parallel (v1 and v1.2) with 107 clinical respiratory samples demonstrated increased bacterial and viral read recovery in v1.2, translating to higher pathogen genome coverage compared to v1. Overall, bacterial sensitivity for v1.2 was 98% compared to 93% for v1, and viral sensitivity was 90% for v1.2 compared to 80% for v1. This multicenter validation has confirmed reproducibility and scalability of the new protocol, establishing a robust framework for clinical implementation of metagenomics.IMPORTANCEThis work represents the validation of an important major update to the protocol used in the United Kingdom National Health Service (NHS) Respiratory Metagenomics service. The service is now deployed in six major hospitals across the UK, and the results of this multicenter validation, as well as showing improved sensitivity, confirm this is a method that is easy to operate and implement in existing hospital laboratories and still provide a same-day turnaround time. The importance of this work is that it provides another step forward to respiratory metagenomics becoming established as a routine clinical diagnostic method.

papers.title: DDR1: a potential pan-cancer prognostic biomarker and therapeutic target in ECM remodeling and CAF infiltration.
papers.abstract: Discoidin domain receptor 1 (DDR1) is implicated in tumor progression, yet its clinical and molecular roles across cancers remain incompletely understood. To address this gap, we conducted a systematic pan-cancer analysis of DDR1 using multiple online databases, including The Cancer Genome Atlas (TCGA), Tumor Immune Estimation Resource 2.0 (TIMER2.0), and cBioPortal for Cancer Genomics, and evaluated its expression, prognostic value, genomic alterations, tumor microenvironment associations, and functional networks. DDR1 was upregulated in 18 cancer types. In survival analyses, high DDR1 expression was significantly associated with favorable overall survival (OS) in kidney renal clear cell carcinoma (KIRC) and mesothelioma (MESO), and with unfavorable disease-free survival (DFS) in cholangiocarcinoma (CHOL), kidney chromophobe (KICH), and KIRC. High DDR1 expression was also associated with advanced pathological stage in several cancer types. Genomic amplification was the predominant alteration. DDR1 expression showed positive correlations with estimated cancer-associated fibroblast (CAF) infiltration in multiple cancer types, although the strength and significance varied by deconvolution algorithm and cancer type. Functional analyses linked DDR1 to extracellular matrix (ECM) regulation and cell migration and proliferation. Notably, no significant correlation was observed between DDR1 and DDR2 expression across cancer types ( R = -0.011, P = 0.26). Whether these two family members have divergent functions warrants further investigation. Collectively, these findings suggest that DDR1 may serve as a potential pan-cancer biomarker and candidate therapeutic target; however, further experimental and clinical validation is required.

papers.title: Rapid detection of the oak wilt pathogen ( Bretziella fagacearum ) using loop-mediated isothermal amplification (LAMP).
papers.abstract: Oak wilt, caused by Bretziella fagacearum , is a destructive disease of Quercus species. Symptoms consist of leaf scorch, dieback, defoliation, vascular discoloration, and eventual death. Prompt diagnosis is crucial for timely management that involves laborious and expensive practices such as sanitation, cutting of infected trees, and proactive tree removal to create a buffer zone, root trenching, and/or fungicide injections. Due to these resource-intensive management tactics, laboratory test accuracy and speed are paramount. Diagnoses of oak wilt currently rely on culturing, nested PCR, or qPCR, but all these methods have limitations, ranging from ambiguous results to high barriers to application. We developed a rapid, robust, and sensitive loop-mediated isothermal amplification (LAMP) diagnostic test using primers and probes that target a section of the internal transcribed spacer region of the rDNA of the oak wilt pathogen , B. fagacearum . This assay can detect B. fagacearum from pure isolates and environmental samples, including branch sapwood, leaf petioles, nitidulid sap beetle vectors, and degraded fungal mats. The LAMP assay developed here is sensitive to a detection limit as low as 1 pg/μL and can detect the pathogen in under 20 min. This real-time LAMP-based diagnostic test is thoroughly validated to specifically detect the oak wilt pathogen, B. fagacearum , and is demonstrated to detect the fungus from a variety of routinely collected sample types.
