Our rapid molecular detection protocol can provide a useful tool for diagnostic labs, forest health practitioners, and researchers studying oak wilt.IMPORTANCEOak wilt is a deadly disease of oaks that represents a growing threat to natural and planted forests throughout eastern North America. To enhance the speed and accuracy of molecular diagnostics for this disease, we designed a molecular test using l oop-mediated isothermal amp lification (LAMP) to reliably and rapidly detect the oak wilt pathogen, Bretziella fagacearum . To optimize the practicality of this assay in real-world conditions, we developed a rigorous validation process that incorporated the known breadth of genetic diversity of the oak wilt pathogen, sample tissue range, and a panel of non-target fungi to assess the potential for false positives. The novel assay is demonstrated to be highly specific and can detect B. fagacearum from host sapwood, leaf petioles, and nitidulid sap beetles, serving as a versatile new tool for forest health surveillance. Our approach also represents a thorough framework for researchers interested in the development of rapid molecular methods for the detection of forest microbes more broadly.

papers.title: Whole-genome analysis uncovers four novel Streptomyces species linked to sweet potato soil rot in China.
papers.abstract: Sweet potato soil rot, caused by pathogenic Streptomyces , is an emerging threat to sweet potato production in China. However, the diversity and pathogenic mechanisms of the associated species remain poorly understood. In this study, symptomatic storage roots exhibiting typical pox-like lesions were collected from major production regions in Henan and Guangdong provinces. A total of 225 actinomycete strains were isolated using optimized methods, and six highly pathogenic strains were identified through tuber slice, hydroponic, and pot inoculation assays. Morphological, physiological, whole-genome sequencing, and phylogenetic analyses revealed considerable diversity among these pathogenic isolates. Average nucleotide identity (ANI) analysis showed that strain (ST10) was closely related to Streptomyces albogriseolus , whereas the remaining strains displayed substantial genomic divergence, indicating diverse taxonomic affiliations. Comparative genomic analysis identified a conserved core genome together with extensive strain-specific gene content, reflecting both functional conservation and adaptive evolution. Phylogenomic analysis placed several isolates close to S. ipomoeae , and others within distinct pathogenic lineages. Notably, none of the six strains possessed the canonical thaxtomin biosynthetic gene cluster, suggesting that pathogenicity is mediated by alternative virulence mechanisms. Instead, conserved gene clusters associated with siderophores and stress-related metabolites were identified, indicating potential roles in host colonization and ecological adaptation. These findings expand our understanding of the genomic diversity and potential pathogenic mechanisms of sweet potato-associated Streptomyces and provide a valuable foundation for disease management and resistance breeding. Herein, we established an optimized isolation method yielding 225 actinomycete strains and a rapid pipeline for pathogenic identification of sweet potato-associated Streptomyces . Six isolates were confirmed as causal agents of sweet potato soil rot, including four novel species. Complete genome sequences of five strains provide a fundamental resource for elucidating pathogenesis mechanisms and advancing taxonomic and evolutionary studies of the genus. The absence of canonical thaxtomin biosynthetic genes across all pathogenic strains, combined with the presence of conserved siderophore and stress-related metabolite clusters, demonstrates that these pathogens utilize alternative virulence mechanisms distinct from well-characterized Streptomyces plant pathogens. Comparative genomics reveals a conserved core genome alongside strain-specific gene content, reflecting functional conservation and adaptive evolution. These genomic resources and experimental validations establish a foundational framework for understanding pathogen diversity, enabling accurate diagnosis of emerging strains and directly informing resistance breeding programs by identifying genetic targets for screening sweet potato germplasm.

papers.title: A Rapid and Portable EmDEA-Based Diagnostic System for On-Site Detection of Erwinia amylovora , the Causal Agent of Fire Blight.
papers.abstract: Fire blight, caused by Erwinia amylovora , is a devastating bacterial disease that primarily affects rosaceous fruit trees, including apple ( Malus spp.) and pear ( Pyrus spp.), and poses a significant threat to global fruit production and orchard management. Effective control depends on precise, sensitive, and practical diagnostic technologies that can be deployed directly in the field. In this study, we developed a portable diagnostic system that enables the rapid and accurate detection of E. amylovora under on-site conditions. The system targets a highly conserved hypothetical protein gene specific to the pathogen, for which six primer pairs and three probes were designed and evaluated. The optimized probe-primer combination demonstrated high specificity, yielding no amplification in 15 nontarget microbial strains or in host plant tissues, and exhibited a sensitivity equivalent to that of quantitative PCR, reliably detecting as little as 100 fg of genomic DNA or 20 colony-forming units per milliliter of bacteria. To streamline sample processing, we employed cellulose filter paper strips to extract DNA within 1 min, achieving detection from leaf surfaces at a sensitivity of 32 colony-forming units per square centimeter. The diagnostic kit is stable at room temperature and, when combined with a palm-sized heating device, allows the entire process from sample preparation to result interpretation to be completed in 5 to 21 min. Field trials further confirmed the suitability of this system for rapid pathogen detection. This study introduces a sensitive, portable, and user-friendly diagnostic platform that enhances fire blight management and provides a framework for developing similar tools against other plant diseases.

papers.title: ARIPA: Agentic Reasoning for Image-based Pathology Analysis
papers.abstract: Nuclear segmentation across patient-derived organoids (PDOs) is complicated by differences in morphology, staining, image scale, and acquisition format. We present ARIPA, an automated human-in-the-loop (HITL) system that coordinates pre-trained segmentation tools through a vision-language model (VLM)-based agentic planning, verification, and refinement loop for hematoxylin and eosin images of formalin-fixed, paraffin-embedded PDOs. In contrast to existing tools, ARIPA does not require training and achieves good performance. Tissue-aware tiling and image-derived calibration initialize segmentation; optional expert corrections guide configuration search and light-weight object-level rules without retraining or fine-tuning the pre-trained segmentation networks. We evaluated initial ARIPA predictions on more than 50,000 nuclei from 19 images of breast, head and neck, and lung patient-derived cancer PDOs, where nuclear segmentation was challenging due to its 3D structure and variation in imaging layers and malignant cell morphology. Performance was evaluated on agent-selected models before expert feedback, after feedback from the initial runs excluding direct expert edits, and in comparison to a custom-trained HoVer-Net model previously published by our group. At a minimum polygon intersection over union (IoU) of 0.5, image-macro F1 was 0.8380 before feedback, 0.9849 after feedback, and 0.4713 for HoVer-Net. Mean area under the F1 score versus IoU curve was 0.8013, 0.9700, and 0.4317, respectively. The mean paired F1 increase after feedback was 0.1468, with increases in 17 out of the total 19 images and no changes in the remaining two. Ground truth nuclei annotations were created by expert review and editing of ARIPA's post-feedback outputs. In this cohort, ARIPA outperformed the custom-trained HoVer-Net, and its performance was improved further following expert-guided HITL refinement. By automatic agentic reasoning with VLM review without training, ARIPA has potential to be rapidly deployed across organs and cancers with HITL design, accelerating the fundamental step towards downstream biomedical applications.

papers.title: In vitro and in vivo validation of recombinant Syrian hamster interferon-α
papers.abstract: The Syrian hamster (Mesocricetus auratus) is an important model for the study of viral pathogenesis and the development of antiviral drugs and vaccines, yet species-specific reagents remain scarce. Here, we validate the potent and specific activity of recombinantly expressed Syrian hamster maIFN-12-like protein (maIFN) in vitro and in vivo. MaIFN expressed in E. coli induced MX2 and ISG15 expression in both BHK21 hamster kidney cells as well as in primary hamster fibroblasts in a dose-dependent manner and EC50 values in low pg/mL range. Activation was strictly STAT2-dependent and more potent, by at least one order of magnitude, than that achieved by heterologous human or mouse IFN. ISG induction translated into a strong antiviral activity against YF17D virus replication in BHK21 cells as well as ISRE-dependent reporter expression in a newly established hamster reporter cell line. When tested in wild-type but not in STAT2-deficient hamsters, maIFN showed a physiologic, vigorous yet rapidly contracting systemic ISG response. Together these findings establish maIFN as a functional antiviral cytokine and valuable reagent for preclinical infectious disease research using Syrian hamsters.

papers.title: Host HSP90 mimicry by a parasite effector triggers mitochondrial membrane shedding
papers.abstract: The outer mitochondrial membrane mediates critical host defenses against intracellular pathogens. How microbes manipulate this compartment remains poorly understood. Here, we found that the human parasite Toxoplasma gondii remodels host mitochondrial membranes through molecular mimicry of HSP90 chaperones. Cryo-electron microscopy analyses showed that the parasite effector TgMAF1 binds the same specialized clamp domain of the mitochondrial import receptor TOM70 as chaperones of the HSP70/90 family. Biochemical and comparative genomics analyses demonstrate that this mimicry arose through the neofunctionalization of the TgMAF1 C-terminus from an ancestral paralog incapable of TOM70 binding. In molecular dynamics simulations, complexed TgMAF1-TOM70 triggered the formation of higher order assemblies that induced local membrane curvature. These findings uncover a previously unknown host subversion strategy and establish molecular mimicry of a chaperone as a mechanism for pathogen-driven remodeling of the host OMM.

papers.title: Saturation mutagenesis and NMR of a fold switch reveal position-dependent deep learning performance
papers.abstract: A predictive understanding of the properties of fold-switching or metamorphic proteins can provide insights into protein dynamics and energetics, and enable the design of complex protein functions and molecular machines. Recently developed deep learning modeling tools, including AlphaFold, have led to dramatic increases in structural modeling accuracy, but their performance for prediction of fold switching or point mutant effects is unclear. Here we used NMR to measure all substitutions at three key positions of the GA/GB fold switch that differentially adopt -helical (3), {beta}-grasp (4{beta}+), or unfolded states, generating a quantitative experimental benchmark for mutation-level fold switching. Using this dataset to assess and compare a panel of deep learning and physics-based modeling and design algorithms, we identified variable and position-dependent performance across methods. Some AlphaFold2-based algorithms were able to predict mutant effects at individual sites, indicating partial sensitivity to physical effects of residue substitutions. Additional comparisons of predictions with experimentally measured stability changes further highlighted position-dependent success and general challenges for predictive algorithms. Together, this study provides a rigorous new benchmark for mutation-induced fold switching and reveals the capabilities and limitations of current deep learning models, establishing a foundational baseline for facilitating the next generation of prediction tools.

papers.title: Resistome-based machine learning source attribution of a superbug
papers.abstract: Many bacterial human pathogens infect not only humans but also other species, and source attribution has been very useful for studying transmission among the different sources. Yet, critical pathogens such as Acinetobacter baumannii have not been studied using source attribution approaches. Here, we conducted machine source attribution using the resistome of almost 1200 A. baumannii genomes from four sources: humans, companion animals , soil, and white storks. Of note, no other study has used the resistome as input data before. First, we selected the best model among 168 parameter combinations, which was Random Forest, with 5-fold cross-validation and chi2 for feature selection. The model shows a reasonably good accuracy with an F1 weighted score = 0.744, yet class accuracy was dependent on the source. Whereas for companion animals and humans, 93% and 86% of the predictions were correct, respectively; the other two categories (soil and white stork) show correct predictions below 50%. Yet, a core phylogeny and ST assignment reveal that the wrong predictions are associated with multi-host lineages. Finally, we identify the most important ARGs contributing to each class prediction and, in the case of companion animals, tetgenes, which confer resistance to tetracycline, were among the top contributors. Our study shows the resistome's potential for developing models to predict source associations. More broadly, this study shows how integrating machine learning and phylogenomics can help us understand multi-host transmission dynamics.

papers.title: Hidden but Expanding Sampling Bias Distorts Prokaryotic Genome Collections
papers.abstract: Public genome collections underpin our understanding of bacterial diversity and the distribution of traits such as antibiotic resistance, and increasingly serve as training data for genomic foundation models. Their growing size promises an increasingly complete view of microbial genetic variation. However, these collections combine studies with different sampling priorities, often overrepresenting subgroups of closely related strains of particular interest. The resulting bias reduces effective information, and its consequences for diversity estimates and the value of further sequencing remain insufficiently quantified. Here we show that accounting for this escalating sampling bias is essential for accurate gene frequency estimates and hints at greater genomic diversity than current data suggest. We propose to detect and reduce sampling bias based on phylogenetic relationships compared to expectations under random sampling, which, in contrast to dereplication and data reduction methods, preserves fine-scale diversity in large samples. Applied to 402 prokaryotic species in the NCBI genome database, our method PhyloThin indicates that the effective number of samples is 41% lower than the actual number but retains more than twice as many genomes as dereplication. Sampling bias varies substantially among species, showing that genome counts alone provide an incomplete measure of how well a species has already been characterized. PhyloThin thus turns biased, expanding genome collections into more representative samples for studying genome evolution and population genetic inference with implications for training genomic foundation models, pathogen surveillance, and the discovery of novel genetic functions.

papers.title: Domain-informed effector gene assignment exposes training-data dependence of drug target prioritisation from GWAS
papers.abstract: About 90% of trait-associated lead variants lie outside protein-coding regions, so nominating the effector gene at genome-wide association study (GWAS) loci remains the principal bottleneck in translating associations into biological insight. Since no experimentally resolved ground truth exists at scale, every method rests on quasi-true-positive sets dominated by a single line of evidence. Here, we benchmarked established prioritisation methods across three independent evaluation sets, trained five models each informed by a different biological domain, and annotated lead variants for six common diseases. Performance did not transfer across domains (AUPRC 0.91 to 0.46 for the same method), and we traced this to how differently models weight the distance between variant and gene (p<5.3x10-123), not to how they were built. Curation assumptions propagated into predictions and can become self-confirming, such as druggability in the Open Targets-informed model. The five models shared only 17.1% to 31.8% of effector gene assignments, converging on established disease biology but diverging where GWAS are expected to yield novel insight. Recovery of 340 approved drug targets differed markedly between models, and no way of combining them, by averaging scores (38.8%) or training on all curations jointly (36.5%), approached the 52.1% recovered across all five together. Our workflow matched Open Targets L2G across three annotation sets without prior biological knowledge and exceeded it where curated knowledge already linked gene and disease. We provide the Domain-informed EFfector gene Assignment framework (DEFA; https://github.com/lkohleick/DEFA), which reports rather than hides the curation assumption behind each gene assignment so that it can be examined and tested.

papers.title: Single-dose neonatal gene therapy preserves motor coordination and extends survival of Polg-deficient mice
papers.abstract: POLG mutations are the most common single nuclear gene cause of mitochondrial disease. POLG disease spans a spectrum of clinical presentations with variable age of onset and severity. Early-onset disease is often severe and fatal (e.g., Alpers syndrome, myocerebrohepatopathy), while late-onset disease can be relatively mild (e.g., progressive external ophthalmoplegia). POLG disease is incurable, with few symptomatic treatments available, none of which can prevent its progression. Gene replacement therapy has the potential to halt or prevent POLG disease, but its development has been hindered by the large size of the POLG cDNA and the scarcity of suitable mouse models. Here, we developed a bespoke Polg knockout (KO) mouse model by inactivating the Polg locus in parvalbumin-expressing neurons (e.g., Purkinje cells) and fast-twitch skeletal muscle fibers. KO mice developed progressive motor coordination deficits, respiratory chain deficiency in Purkinje cells and skeletal muscle, and died prematurely. We also developed nine AAV-based gene therapy vectors and confirmed their ability to deliver and express the human POL{gamma}A protein in different mouse tissues. A single high-dose administration of either of two lead candidates into Polg KO neonates preserved respiratory chain activity in Purkinje cells and skeletal muscle, delayed the onset of motor coordination deficits, and extended lifespan. Thus, our work provides preclinical proof of concept for gene replacement therapy for POLG disease, establishing the feasibility of this approach and laying the foundation for further development in the field.

papers.title: Accurate and interpretable protein complex stoichiometry prediction through agentic AI with StoiAgent
papers.abstract: Accurate protein complex structure modeling requires knowledge of complex stoichiometry, yet the copy numbers of individual subunits are often unknown. Consequently, predicting protein complex stoichiometry has emerged as a major challenge in recent years. Here, we present StoiAgent, a large language model (LLM)-powered AI agent that automates the retrieval and integration of sequence, structural, and literature evidence to predict stoichiometry while preserving interpretable reasoning traces (chain of thoughts) of its evidence assessment and ranking decision. An open-weight LLM model, Qwen3.6-27B, is used by StoiAgent as the LLM backbone to combine sequences, structural templates, AlphaFold3 structure predictions, and literature evidence, and perform stoichiometry candidate generation and ranking. On 56 CASP17 protein complex targets, it achieves top-1 accuracy of 75.0%, which represents a 23.2 percentage-point improvement over PreStoi with AlphaFold3 ranking (51.8%) and matches the top-1 accuracy of StoPred. Moreover, StoiAgent has a higher top-3 and top-5 accuracy than StoPred (85.7% versus 80.4% and 87.5% versus 85.7%, respectively). Furthermore, it outperforms general-purpose frontier LLMs, including ChatGPT and Gemini, in stoichiometry prediction. Case studies further illustrate how StoiAgent evaluates competing assembly hypotheses by integrating complementary evidence, with recorded reasoning traces documenting its decision-making process. Overall, StoiAgent demonstrates the potential of LLM-powered AI agents to improve protein complex stoichiometry prediction through the automated integration of diverse sources of evidence while providing interpretable explanations to guide downstream structure modeling.

papers.title: GENECraft: A Function- and Prior-Constrained Discrete Dynamical System for Controllable Regulatory DNA Design
papers.abstract: Designing regulatory DNA requires reconciling two complementary modeling paradigms: genomic language models (gLMs) capture evolutionary syntax without guaranteeing targeted regulatory activity, whereas sequence-to-function predictors provide explicit functional supervision without enforcing native-like sequence plausibility. We introduce GENECraft, a training-free Function- and Prior-Constrained Discrete Dynamical System (FP-DDS) that couples a genomic language model (Carbon) and a functional oracle (AlphaGenome) during inference-time optimization to balance predicted regulatory activity and consistency with genomic sequence priors. GENECraft evolves continuous latent nucleotide logits while evaluating strictly decoded discrete DNA sequences under a time-dependent composite vector field that fuses normalized functional utility, bidirectional contextual prior guidance, and compositional quality penalties, followed by feasibility-first trajectory readout. Across 2,185 loci spanning promoters, multi-constraint enhancers, and 18 transcription factors (TFs), GENECraft achieves full-joint success rates of 62.70%, 65.23%, and 94.56% (macro-averaged), substantially outperforming seven optimization, evolutionary, and generative baselines (which reach at most 2.15% on enhancers). In matched 336-locus ablations, in-loop Carbon guidance reduces native-relative dinucleotide divergence by 7.8--11.5%, enhancer context sensitivity by 10.5%, and TF mutation sensitivity by 11.0%, establishing FP-DDS as a principled framework for controllable regulatory DNA design.

papers.title: Genomes to Fields 2026: Genomic resources for investigating genotype-phenotype relationships in Zea mays
papers.abstract: Maize (Zea mays L.) is a major global crop characterized by high genetic and phenotypic diversity across accessions. To better understand this diversity, the Genomes-to-Fields initiative has produced paired genotypic and phenotypic datasets annually since 2014. Here, we present 15 genome assemblies representing 13 maize lines, including founders and testers from the 2022-2023, 2024-2025, and 2026-2027 Genomes-to-Fields evaluation cycles and additional breeding germplasm, together with gene and repeat annotations. Assemblies ranged from 2.19 to 2.38 Gb, with BUSCO completeness of 97.9-99.0%. Excluding the more fragmented LH287 assembly (contig N50 = 5.3 Mb; 90.8% chromosome placement), contig N50 values ranged from 31.1 to 195.8 Mb, with 95.9-99.4% of sequence placed on chromosomes. Gene annotation identified approximately 40,000 gene models per genotype, of which 93.6-93.9% were classified as protein-coding, with 95.9-97.3% complete BUSCOs. Comparison with B73 identified 27,606-30,517 one-to-one syntenic orthologs per genotype, representing 69.4-76.8% of B73 genes. Transposable elements occupied 83.6-88.6% of the genomes, with LTR retrotransposons representing the predominant class. Comparative genome alignments revealed three large inversions, including a 12.65-Mb inversion on chromosome 3 present in six of the 13 lines. Together, these resources expand the genomic representation of maize breeding germplasm and provide a foundation for investigating genetic variation underlying agronomic traits.

papers.title: Measuring the information budget of cross-target antibody affinity generalization: a robust cross-target wall, and why structure reaches developability but not affinity
papers.abstract: Structure-based machine learning is widely expected to advance antibody engineering, yet it is unclear how far affinity predictions transfer to new targets, and why. We introduce a noise-corrected, censoring-aware estimator of the cross-target transfer ceiling, {rho}max = {surd}(T/(T+I)), which separates a transferable antibody-intrinsic component (T) from a non-transferable target-specific interaction (I). On deterministic synthetic ground truth the estimator recovers the noise-free ceiling to {+/-} 0.0003, whereas the naive sum-of-squares estimator is biased downward by measurement noise. Applying it from synthetic to real systems, the transferable budget is small, and on real neutralization panels it is not an artefact: the target-specific interaction survives noise and censoring correction. It is strongly regime-dependent, with a two-tier structure: predicting a novel antibody from sequence alone (the design setting) reaches a lower ceiling ({rho} {approx} 0.44 on real breadth data) than ranking a characterized one ({rho} {approx} 0.59), even with a strong protein language model. Synthetic oracles also overstate transferability: an oracle scored on real predicted structures carries about half the budget of a matched synthetic lattice (0.45 vs. 0.81), and real neutralization and escape panels sit well below the synthetic ceiling (0.32-0.68). Under leakage-free antigen-cluster splits, cross-target affinity ranking across every method family collapses to this budget, while within a sampled target a structure-based graph network ranks affinity above off-the-shelf FoldX and GearBind (within-complex Spearman 0.55), and structural surface descriptors predict a surface-driven developability property (hydrophobic aggregation) where sequence-dominated properties (humanness, charge-driven self-association) do not benefit. A controlled ablation attributes the residual within-target signal to the antibody alone: dropping the antigen from the structural model leaves it essentially unchanged (interface {Delta} {rho} between -0.01 and +0.02 across four panels), so for this model the paratope-epitope interface adds no ranking signal over the antibody alone. Models climb toward the budget within a target -- via a measure-then-rank operating mode that recovers top binders 6-8 times more efficiently than random once a target has been sampled -- but none crosses it.

papers.title: Fine-tuned DNA sequence language models for predicting gene expression in admixed population: A comparison with variant-based methods
papers.abstract: Predicting gene expression from whole genome sequencing data is essential for elucidating regulatory mechanisms and interpreting functional consequences of non-coding variants to complex diseases. While traditional approaches rely on variant-based linear models, DNA sequence-based language models have gained increasing popularity for their ability to learn regulatory features directly from whole genome sequence data. Previous studies have evaluated models such as Enformer, but newer sequence-to-function models, including Borzoi and AlphaGenome, remain less well characterized for individual-level gene expression prediction, particularly in non-European and admixed populations. Here, we evaluated and fine-tuned Borzoi and AlphaGenome using personal genomes paired with whole-blood RNA-seq data from the Hispanic Community Health Study/Study of Latinos (HCHS/SOL). Fine-tuning substantially improved the performance of both sequence-based models compared with their pretrained versions; however, their performances remained similar to that of the variant-based linear models. Leveraging the ancestral diversity of HCHS/SOL, we found that Borzoi and AlphaGenome showed similar performance across Amerindian-, European-, and African-enriched groups. Fine-tuned Borzoi, fine-tuned AlphaGenome and elastic net performed modestly better when trained and evaluated in the same ancestry-enriched group. Finally, we explored strategies to improve prediction performance and found that incorporating predicted epigenetic features improved prediction near the promoter region. Significant progress remains needed before the full potential of sequence-based models is attained. Incorporating more biology-guided training approaches could be helpful to achieving better performance.

papers.title: BiomedCAT: Biomedical Context Analysis Tool for Supporting Mechanistic Hypothesis Generation via User-defined Contextual Subgraph Extraction
papers.abstract: Researchers formulate mechanistic hypotheses in slides and figures long before they write them as text, yet knowledge-graph (KG) tools expect a query in the vocabulary of the graph. We present BiomedCAT, an open-source workflow that turns biomedical slides into a subgraph of the RTX-KG2c knowledge graph shaped by the user's research profile, on a laptop and without sending the documents out. A small vision-language model describes each slide; a 4-billion-parameter agent types the terms into the classes of the Biolink model; an existence gate removes invented entities; identifiers are retrieved from Translator services or from a local table and selected, never generated, by a judge model; and a profile-weighted two-hop expansion builds the context graph. On a synthetic Biolink typing benchmark whose labels were audited by an expert, the local agent reaches 0.71 accuracy on 517 non-ambiguous mentions, 4 points below Claude Opus 5 (0.75), level with DeepSeek-V4-Flash (0.69) and above open-weight models of 24 and 31 billion parameters; the audit also showed that 55\% of the generated labels were wrong or ambiguous. On expert-annotated slide decks, the reading stage recovers 81 to 94\% of the explicit terms of the English deck, less on French decks, and linking assigns the expert identifier to 65\% of the found terms online and 26\% in the fully local mode. A one-slide run takes 33 to 42 minutes, with peaks of 9.8~GB of system RAM above idle and 5.3~GB of GPU memory. In a facioscapulohumeral muscular dystrophy (FSHD) case, three slides that each draw one pathway from DUX4 at a different biological scale give graphs that overlap by 7 to 15\% of their nodes, each recovering its own pathway's expected nodes, and expose sourced paths from DUX4, such as a DUX4--HMGB1 interaction from IntAct. Of 21 compounds tested in FSHD, seven, including every agent that targets DUX4, are absent from RTX-KG2c, which bounds what a graph-based approach can propose. BiomedCAT lets a researcher set a working hypothesis against curated knowledge, with every edge traceable to its source.

papers.title: XAMPGen: An Interpretable Super Intelligence Pipeline For Novel Antimicrobial Peptide Discovery
papers.abstract: Antimicrobial peptides (AMPs) are short peptides with a broad spectrum of activity against bacterial pathogens, representing a promising avenue for combating the growing threat of antibiotic resistance. This study focuses on two main components: 1) generative super intelligence (GenSI) and 2) utilizing explainable super intelligence (XSI). We fine-tuned ProGen, a decoder-only protein language model, on known AMPs to generate novel peptide sequences with strong antimicrobial properties. Generated candidates were screened with an AMP classifier and filtered based on predicted minimum inhibitory concentration (MIC), along with human insights into AMP structure and activity in bacterial membranes. A final set of peptides was selected for synthesis and experimental testing. Biological assays confirmed antimicrobial activity in all generated and tested peptides, while fluorescence and circular dichroism measurements characterized membrane binding and peptide structure. We then applied XSI techniques to interpret the generative model and derive biological insights. Specifically, layer probing was used to identify cornerstone layers that encode functionally critical information. Self-attention analysis within these layers revealed residue-level interdependencies and patterns underlying antimicrobial functions, which we evaluated against well-characterized AMPs from the literature. We further examined associations between amino acid sequence patterns and binding properties in bacterial membrane mimics, relating these observations to biological activities in cell-based assays. These analyses provide insight into the model's decision-making process. This builds confidence that the learned amino acid interdependencies have physico-chemical significance, as applied to AMPs, and may facilitate the discovery of novel AMPs with therapeutic potential. This work demonstrates that interpretable generative language models can support rational AMP discovery.

papers.title: Computable Genomes: A Layered Computational Framework for Non-Coding DNA and Cellular Behavior
papers.abstract: Genome-wide association studies have catalogued tens of thousands of trait-associated loci, most of them in non-coding DNA, yet for most loci the path from nucleotide to phenotype remains correlational. We propose a layered computational decomposition of the genome as a complement to data-driven approaches: sequence as formal language, sequence as information-bearing signal, mobile elements as runtime, compilation to interaction networks through thermodynamic and rule-based models, and execution as cellular and multicellular dynamics. Each layer is defined by its inputs, outputs and formalisms, and we set out where the frame breaks down, including the looseness of algorithmic-information estimates, the triviality of universality results and the failure of string grammars at the chromatin level. Synthetic-biology platforms serve as tests of whether the layers compose, and genomic foundation models and the AlphaGenome Atlas, which predicts effects for all nine billion possible single-nucleotide variants, serve as oracles whose coverage and limits we map onto the framework. We state five falsifiable predictions and test the first, that sequence compressibility carries information about regulatory function beyond composition and conservation, on 38,556 single-nucleotide variants from a saturation-mutagenesis reporter assay of 21 regulatory elements. In a pooled model, local compressibility is associated with measured effect size (standardized {beta} = -0.030, p = 0.0014). The association roughly halves under full control for base composition, loses significance when composition, motif and noise adjustments are combined under locus-level inference (wild cluster bootstrap p = 0.11), and averages zero within loci (random-effects {beta} = -0.0003, p = 0.90). The prediction is therefore not supported at the variant level in these data, which bound the effect a genome-wide test should expect. The argument is not that the genome "is" a program, but that treating it as one supplies formal tools whose predictions can be checked.

papers.title: SPIDER: Contextualizing Biomedical Knowledge for Evidence-Grounded Scientific Reasoning
papers.abstract: Aggregated relations in biomedical knowledge graphs can obscure evidence and study conditions, complicating the distinction between scientific disagreement and contextual differences. Here we introduce SPIDER, a multi-agent framework grounding biomedical relations in literature evidence and extracting study conditions for interpretation. Applied to a graph integrating 48 databases and ontologies, SPIDER analyzed 1.95 million PubMed abstracts, adding 2.31 million previously unrepresented, literature-supported entity pairs to construct SPIDER-KG. Daily updates incorporate relations and evidence from newly indexed PubMed records. Across 89,937 evidence-supported comparisons of potentially incompatible relations, SPIDER classified 79.0% as contextual differences, and 6.1% as genuine disagreement, achieving 80.3% macro-F1 averaged across both categories against expert annotations. On SPIDER-Bench and four biomedical reasoning benchmarks, SPIDER-KG improved large language models' interpretation of evidence-supported biomedical relationships. Retrospective analysis of newly reported gene--disease relationships further demonstrated how evidence-linked knowledge can contextualize emerging discoveries. SPIDER-KG provides a reusable, incrementally extensible evidence layer for biomedical reasoning.

papers.title: Multimodal Structural and Regulatory Architecture of Coding and Non-Coding Variants Across the Orofacial Clefting TP63-IRF6-GRHL3 Network
papers.abstract: Pathogenic variation across the TP63-IRF6-GRHL3 transcriptional network causes syndromic and nonsyndromic orofacial clefts (OFCs), yet scalar sequence predictors collapse distinct failure modes and leave isoform-specific coding variants, splice-altering indels, and distal enhancer alleles unresolved. Here, we integrate 29 AlphaFold 3 (AF3) assemblies (10 wild-type, 19 mutant), thermodynamic stability ({Delta}{Delta}G) calculations, and AlphaGenome regulatory modeling across clinical, saturation-mutagenesis, and reporter benchmarks. In strict leave-one-gene-out (LOGO) coding benchmarks, replacing paralog crystal templates with full-length human AF3 structures improves IRF6 classification (biophysical AUROC rising from 0.7844 to 0.8967; {Delta}{Delta}G from 0.6461 to 0.8516) and resolves canonical isoform gaps in the 602-residue MANE Select GRHL3 homodimer. Projecting IRF6 missense variants onto a two-dimensional stability-versus-interface phase plane separates dominant-negative popliteal pterygium syndrome (PPS) poisons from haploinsufficient Van der Woude syndrome (VWS1) alleles (VWS1-versus-PPS Quadrant I odds ratio [OR] = 0.0263 [reciprocal OR = 38.0], p = 4.652 x 10-3) and distinguishes DNA-contact poisons from dimer-unfolding alleles across 12 zebrafish in vivo assays. Atomistic base-readout contacts in the AF3 TP63-MCS9.7 tetramer mirror loss-of-function profiles in MaveDB ({rho} = 0.6048, p = 6.52 x 10-4) and AlphaGenome keratinocyte DNase predictions ({rho} = 0.6040, p = 6.65 x 10-4). Across non-coding benchmarks, AlphaGenome splicing tracks reach an AUROC of 0.9876 while prioritizing cryptic splice variants of uncertain significance, and epithelial chromatin tracks capture enhancer grammar, plasmid-cloning artifacts, and context-dependent ARHGAP29, FOXE1, and local 8q24 chromatin effects within AlphaGenome's 1.049-Mb horizon.

papers.title: Benchmarking four large language models on generating and selecting hypotheses that match published findings in 50 studies of ageing biology
papers.abstract: Objective We asked how often hypotheses generated by large language models for 50 research tasks matched the withheld finding of the published study, and whether model forecasts could identify the matching hypotheses. Methods We built tasks from 50 peer-reviewed studies in ageing biology published after the models' stated training cutoffs; each task gave the background and a research question and withheld the study's finding (the reference finding). GPT-6 Astra, Grok 4.5, Claude Opus 5.5, and Gemini 4 Argon each generated five hypotheses per task by three methods: a single request, a multistep pipeline, and the Omega Point method without literature search (2997 hypotheses). A hypothesis matched the reference finding if at least two of three judge models from other developers scored it at least 3 (primary threshold) or at least 4 (strict threshold) on a 0 to 5 scale; refusals counted as non-matches. A selection rule, chosen from 112 variants evaluated on the Grok 4.5 hypotheses, kept only the hypotheses for which all four predictor models forecast experimental confirmation; the predictors never saw the published finding. The controls were recorded random answers and each generator's first-listed hypothesis. Confidence intervals (95% CIs) were calculated by cluster bootstrap over tasks. Results Of the hypotheses generated by a single request, 13.2% to 18.0% matched the reference finding, compared with 11.2% to 18.8% for the multistep pipeline and 2.8% to 7.6% for the Omega Point method. With a single request, the hypothesis listed first matched in 37.5% of cases (75/200), and the hypotheses in positions 2 to 5 matched in 10.1% (81/800). Among the hypotheses selected unanimously, the match rate was 73.7% (14/19) for Grok 4.5, 47.4% (9/19) for Gemini 4 Argon, and 63.6% (14/22) for Claude Opus 5.5, compared with 12.1% to 17.9% for the random control and 37.5% to 40.0% for the first-listed hypotheses. The selected lists captured 27.3% to 35.0% of all matching hypotheses. Pooled across the three sets, the match rate among selected hypotheses exceeded that among first-listed hypotheses by 23.2 percentage points (pp; 95% CI [13.0, 32.6]). When Gemini 4 Argon re-extracted the reference findings, the match rate among selected hypotheses was 59.6% (34/57), compared with 61.4% (35/57) against the original reference findings for the same tasks. In a manual audit with the generator, judge scores, and selection status hidden, our classifications agreed with the judges' at the primary threshold in 81/100 cases (Cohen's kappa 0.62). Agreement was 89.7% after weighting the sample strata by their size in the corpus. We classified 19 of 30 sampled selected hypotheses as matches, and the judges classified 20 of 30. Conclusions In the evaluated sets, unanimous selection by the four predictors increased the match rate among selected hypotheses; the resulting match rate depended on the matching threshold. Generators listed a matching hypothesis first more often than in later positions, and 50 of the 60 selected hypotheses were listed first. The advantage over the first-listed hypotheses and over the best single predictor at equal list length was statistically significant for the Grok and Opus hypotheses but not for the Gemini hypotheses, and the pairwise differences of the advantage between generators were not statistically significant (p >= 0.16 after Holm correction). We selected the rule using the Grok hypotheses and evaluated it on the Gemini and Opus hypotheses for the same 50 tasks; it has not been tested on new tasks.

papers.title: Cumulative antibiograms: effects of isolate selection and stratification order on susceptibility estimates and resistance representation
papers.abstract: Cumulative antibiograms depend on how isolates are selected and how data are stratified. Different selection strategies may affect both the number of isolates included and the susceptibility estimates reported. We retrospectively analyzed routine microbiology records from a tertiary-care hospital in Barcelona, Spain (2022-2025). Within each patient-organism-calendar-year unit, we compared three isolate-selection strategies: first-isolate, resistance-phenotype, and susceptibility-profile. We assessed the number of isolates retained, susceptibility at standard or increased exposure, the identification of resistance-phenotype profiles, and the effect of de-duplication before versus after stratification. Annual differences in susceptibility were estimated using paired cluster-bootstrap confidence intervals. For Pseudomonas aeruginosa, susceptibility-profile selection retained 16.9% more isolates than first-isolate selection, with differences exceeding 5 percentage points in 10 of 44 annual antimicrobial comparisons. No annual susceptibility differences exceeding this threshold were observed for the other species. Resistance-phenotype and susceptibility-profile selection criteria identified 468 MDR and 278 XDR P. aeruginosa isolates. Of these, 90 (19.2%) of the MDR and 53 (19.1%) of the XDR isolates were not captured by first-isolate selection. In the broader stratification dataset, stratification-first processing increased first-isolate retention by 21.2% for blood specimens and 11.2% for inpatients. These findings show that modest changes in cumulative susceptibility can coexist with incomplete representation of resistant phenotypes. In conclusion, phenotype- and AST-profile-based selection capture additional resistance information beyond first-isolate selection, despite modest differences in cumulative susceptibility. Clinical validation is needed before their use to guide empirical therapy.

papers.title: AmyloCore-ML: AI/Machine Learning Enabled Identification of Amyloid Fibril Core Regions Using Protein Language Models
papers.abstract: Identification of amyloid forming regions in proteins remains central to understanding of their aggregation behaviour, which are central to various neurodegenerative and systemic disorders. Many predictors have been designed to identify amyloid forming regions, however they may not necessarily identify total residues found in actual disease associated fibril structures. To address this, we formed a sequence-based based predictor-AmyloCore-ML to ascertain structural amyloid-core propensity. The predictor was developed using experimentally determined fibril structures obtained from Amyloid Atlas. Ordered residues in the experimental structures were designated as core, and unresolved sampled from the same proteins as matched controls as non-core. Core and non-core regions were encoded using various physicochemical descriptors and protein language model (PLM) embeddings (ESM-2, ANKH, ProtT5) and evaluated using protein-grouped cross-validation. PLMs consistently outperformed physicochemical descriptors, with the best models reaching AUROC values of ~0.88 and AUPRC values of ~0.85. Locked full-length protein scans further localized experimental cores, with ESM-2/ExtraTrees achieving AUROC 0.833, AUPRC 0.751, and a mean peak distance of 12.4 residues. In comparative benchmarking, our predictor showed better performance metrics than CrossBeta and AggrescanAI. The framework therefore provides residue-resolved prediction of structurally incorporated amyloid-core regions directly from sequence.

papers.title: Single-dose neonatal gene therapy preserves motor coordination and extends survival of Polg-deficient mice
papers.abstract: POLG mutations are the most common single nuclear gene cause of mitochondrial disease. POLG disease spans a spectrum of clinical presentations with variable age of onset and severity. Early-onset disease is often severe and fatal (e.g., Alpers syndrome, myocerebrohepatopathy), while late-onset disease can be relatively mild (e.g., progressive external ophthalmoplegia). POLG disease is incurable, with few symptomatic treatments available, none of which can prevent its progression. Gene replacement therapy has the potential to halt or prevent POLG disease, but its development has been hindered by the large size of the POLG cDNA and the scarcity of suitable mouse models. Here, we developed a bespoke Polg knockout (KO) mouse model by inactivating the Polg locus in parvalbumin-expressing neurons (e.g., Purkinje cells) and fast-twitch skeletal muscle fibers. KO mice developed progressive motor coordination deficits, respiratory chain deficiency in Purkinje cells and skeletal muscle, and died prematurely. We also developed nine AAV-based gene therapy vectors and confirmed their ability to deliver and express the human POL{gamma}A protein in different mouse tissues. A single high-dose administration of either of two lead candidates into Polg KO neonates preserved respiratory chain activity in Purkinje cells and skeletal muscle, delayed the onset of motor coordination deficits, and extended lifespan. Thus, our work provides preclinical proof of concept for gene replacement therapy for POLG disease, establishing the feasibility of this approach and laying the foundation for further development in the field.

papers.title: nf-core/pairgenomealign: a scalable pipeline for pairwise whole-genome alignment
papers.abstract: Genome assemblies are accumulating rapidly across the Tree of Life, creating a growing need for reproducible and scalable methods for whole-genome comparison. We developed nf-core/pairgenomealign, a Nextflow workflow that automates pairwise genome alignment using the LAST software suite and produces standard alignment, visualisation, and summary outputs. The pipeline supports a wide range of evolutionary distances, runs reproducibly across local, cloud, and high-performance computing environments, and exports alignments in formats including MAF, BAM, BCF, and CRAM. We repurposed the compact format used for sequencing reads to combine the alignments of many genomes to the same target into a single file, which genome browsers display directly and from which multiple sequence alignments of any region can be extracted. Benchmarking against established genome aligners shows competitive performance with tunable trade-offs between speed and sensitivity, while applications to comparative genomics and assembly quality control illustrate its uses.

papers.title: A modular workflow for biomedical entity normalization across heterogeneous biological ontologies
papers.abstract: Understanding the biological mechanisms underlying rare diseases requires integrating information about phenotypes, cell types, anatomical structures, and molecular functions and processes. Although some of this knowledge is available in structured resources, additional relationships remain dispersed across biomedical literature. Extracting and integrating this information requires normalizing heterogeneous biological entities against specialized ontologies. This motivated the development of a common biomedical named entity normalization (NEN) workflow and the evaluation of its performance across different entity types and ontologies. We developed a modular NEN workflow combining exact matching, lexical and semantic candidate retrieval, and reranking, without requiring ontology-specific training. Candidate retrieval integrates BM25, fuzzy matching, character n-gram similarity, and SapBERT. We evaluated the workflow across the Human Phenotype Ontology (HPO), Cell Ontology (CL), Uberon, and Gene Ontology (GO) using multiple benchmarks, separately assessing candidate retrieval, reranking accuracy, and overall normalization accuracy. We also investigated factors associated with retrieval difficulty and compared the workflow with CellExLink, a specialized cell-type normalization system. Retrieval performance varied across ontologies and benchmarks, with lexical and semantic methods providing complementary candidate coverage in some settings. Increasing candidate-set size improved retrieval recall but did not necessarily improve overall normalization accuracy, as larger candidate sets could reduce reranking performance. Retrieval difficulty was associated with mention characteristics and ontology categories. Our evaluation identifies the performance characteristics and limitations of a common normalization workflow across heterogeneous biological ontologies, highlighting the importance of assessing candidate retrieval and selection separately. The workflow provides a methodological foundation for extracting and integrating biological information from rare disease literature, with potential applicability to other biomedical information-extraction tasks requiring normalization against these ontologies.

papers.title: Generation of a Public Dataset for Etiological Subtyping with the Genomic Cluster Engine
papers.abstract: Motivation: Genetic diseases are complex phenomena that are currently defined by their clinical symptoms, rather than by the combinations of variants that give rise to them. Incomplete penetrance and phenotypic variability indicate that the genomic background contributes to the effect of variants. Recent advancements in genomics have produced vast amounts of data and created new opportunities to study genetic diversity across human populations. Much of this variation is inherited as recombination-defined contiguous segments, called haploblocks. We previously introduced a novel methodology for genomic hash encoding, the Genomic Cluster Engine, which groups individuals into clusters using phased haploblock sequences. By encoding each haploblock sequence as a compact hash, the characterization of genomic backgrounds, the subtyping of etiologies and the inference of local ancestry become fast and scalable. Results: We have optimized the Genomic Cluster Engine pipeline for large genomic datasets through parallelization and improved memory management. We applied our pipeline to 2,548 individuals across 26 populations from the 1000 Genomes Project and produced a dataset of haploblock-based genomic hashes for the resulting clusters. The genomic hashes and clusters can be used for investigating variant effects in the context of their haplotype backgrounds or for genotype-phenotype association studies. This comprehensive dataset is now publicly available, providing a valuable resource for both academic and industry researchers worldwide. Availability: The haploblock boundaries, sequences, clusters and genomic hashes for the 1000 Genomes Project are available under the CC0 license at https://data.haploblocks.org and on the Registry of Open Data on AWS https://registry.opendata.aws.

papers.title: Agentic AI versus pediatric emergency physicians for differential diagnosis of acutely ill and injured children
papers.abstract: Background Misdiagnosis and delayed diagnosis of children in pediatric emergency departments lead to complications, and are particularly problematic in settings with limited pediatric expertise. Large language models (LLMs) have shown promise in diagnostic reasoning for adult emergency department patients, but utility for pediatric cases is largely untested. Methods Retrospective study of patients seen in the emergency department of a major urban pediatric academic medical center and subsequently admitted to the operating room or inpatient service. Records from 100 patients were randomly selected, stratified by age. We compared the accuracy of differential diagnoses (up to five, ranked by likelihood) generated by an LLM agent, Dr CaBot (one configuration with literature search, the other without), with those of four attending pediatric emergency medicine physicians (diagnosticians), all masked to outcome. Encounters were presented to diagnosticians stepwise across four touchpoints: triage, the initial physician evaluation (the a priori primary touchpoint), the full emergency department encounter, and the admission. Ground truth diagnosis was determined by two independent, board-certified pediatric emergency physicians (reviewers) based on the entire clinical encounter. The reviewers, masked to source, then assigned each differential a Bond score (0 to 5; 4 or above was high-scoring). Findings The median patient age was 4 years and 41% had a complex chronic condition. Bond score agreement between the two reviewers had a weighted kappa of 0.64. For the primary comparison at the initial physician evaluation touchpoint, the LLM agent and the diagnosticians both achieved high-scoring differentials in 95% of cases (difference 0%, 95%CI: -5.8, 5.8%). No differences were detected at the other touchpoints. Interpretation Dr CaBot and attending pediatric emergency medicine physicians showed similar performance in generating differential diagnoses from clinical documentation, suggesting potential as a diagnostic aid. Whether this performance improves care, particularly outside pediatric specialty centers, requires prospective evaluation.

papers.title: Genome-resolved metagenomics reveals population-dependent gut microbiome responses to albendazole-ivermectin treatment
papers.abstract: Soil-transmitted helminth control relies on mass anthelmintic treatment, yet helminth-anthelmintic-microbiome interactions and their role on treatment response remain poorly understood. We characterised the microbiome, resistome, and functional profiles of 858 paired stool metagenomes from 429 children treated with albendazole or a fixed-dose albendazole-ivermectin co-formulation in the ALIVE clinical trial in Ethiopia and Mozambique. Baseline microbiome composition differed more by country than infection status and was not associated with albendazole efficacy or adverse events. Co-formulation treatment, particularly three consecutive daily doses, was associated with depletion of Enterobacteriaceae, predominantly Escherichia coli, in Ethiopia, with reductions in E. coli-associated resistance genes and metabolic pathways. Genome-resolved analyses of over 22,000 high-quality metagenome-assembled genomes confirmed this depletion across multiple E. coli strain-level populations, linking taxonomic, resistome, and functional signals to one ecological event. These findings reveal an off-target effect of combination anthelmintic treatment relevant to large-scale deworming programmes and expand genomic resources for African gut microbiota.

papers.title: HLA-Resolve: Four-field HLA typing and MHC variant detection from long-read hybrid capture
papers.abstract: The major histocompatibility complex (MHC) is among the most polymorphic and difficult-to-genotype regions of the human genome. Accurate typing of its HLA genes, which encode antigen-presenting molecules, is critical for transplantation, pharmacogenomics, and disease-risk prediction. Long-read sequencing is increasingly used in HLA typing because of its ability to phase variants across long distances, but many long-read HLA typing workflows still rely on long-range PCR. Here, we present an end-to-end workflow for MHC genotyping that pairs hybrid capture with long-read sequencing on PacBio or Oxford Nanopore, using single-step enzymatic fragmentation and barcoding to enable automated library preparation. The hybrid capture panel enriches both classical and non-classical HLA Class I and Class II genes, as well as all 69 protein-coding MHC Class III genes. We introduce HLA-Resolve, a bioinformatic tool that types HLA genes from PacBio reads via phased full-gene sequence reconstruction, and we benchmark the capture assay and HLA-Resolve together across 32 geographically diverse samples. With PacBio data, variant calling achieved F1 scores of 99.8% for SNVs and 98.4% for indels against the Genome in a Bottle benchmark. HLA-Resolve showed 99.5% allele concordance with reference typings from the International Histocompatibility Working Group and the Human Pangenome Reference Consortium (HPRC) at three-field resolution and 90.5% at four-field resolution, outperforming three other open-source long-read HLA typers on our HiFi hybrid capture reads. The full-gene sequences reconstructed by HLA-Resolve showed zero edit distance to the corresponding HPRC assemblies in 95% of comparisons. HLA-Resolve also showed high accuracy with whole-genome sequencing (WGS) data, achieving 99.4% two-field concordance across 146 public PacBio WGS libraries and 99.5% three-field concordance across the 52 with full-resolution reference typings. Although developed for the MHC, the workflow is customizable to any gene set, providing a general framework for high-resolution genotyping.

papers.title: Prospective prediction of clinical trial outcomes from public evidence
papers.abstract: Predicting clinical trial outcomes requires interpreting biological and clinical evidence in the context of a specific intervention, population and study design. Here we test whether a general-purpose large language model (LLM) can predict trial outcomes from publicly available evidence. We introduce TrialDossier, which assembles standardized evidence dossiers, and TrialOutlook, which uses these dossiers with GPT-5 to estimate the probability that a trial meets its prespecified primary endpoint. Among 694 ongoing trials with results expected within six months of cohort assembly, 69 outcomes first disclosed after forecast recording had been adjudicated by 20 October 2026. TrialOutlook achieved an area under the receiver operating characteristic curve of 0.819 (95% confidence interval, 0.708 to 0.914) and an average precision of 0.860. TrialOutlook correctly identified 27 of 29 failures (93.1%) and incorrectly classified 17 of 40 successes as failures. We further recorded forecasts for 5,809 ongoing trials associated with US-listed companies and established a public benchmark linking archived evidence and fixed forecasts to adjudicated outcomes as they become available.

papers.title: Virtual spatial transcriptomics links kidney histopathology to disease-associated molecular programs
papers.abstract: Introduction: Spatial transcriptomics can resolve compartment-specific molecular programs in kidney disease, but its cost and technical requirements limit its use in clinical diagnostics and in large biopsy archives. Predicting spatial gene expression from routine histology with artificial intelligence could extend molecular characterization to existing clinically annotated kidney tissue collections. Methods: We adapted DeepSpot-M, a pretrained multimodal foundation model that predicts spatial gene expression from histology, using paired hematoxylin and eosin images and Visium spatial transcriptomics from 209 Kidney Precision Medicine Project (KPMP) participants. We evaluated virtual profiles in held-out human biopsies, associated them with histopathologic and biochemical injury markers in 567 rats with defined nephrotoxin exposures from a public toxicogenomics database, and generated a virtual atlas from 1,534 histology slides of 476 additional KPMP participants. Results: Kidney-specific adaptation of DeepSpot-M doubled the mean Pearson correlation of each model's 1,000 best-predicted genes (0.43 versus 0.22) and exceeded recent foundation models. Virtual profiles preserved the direction of all 13 disease-marker differences in measured expression, including tubular injury, maladaptive repair, gluconeogenesis, and fibrosis-associated programs. All 11 measured associations between molecular programs and estimated glomerular filtration rate (eGFR) were also preserved. Without rat-specific training, a virtual injury score distinguished moderate or severe histopathologic lesions (area under the curve, 0.85) and at least twofold blood urea nitrogen elevation (0.82). In our atlas of 5.46 million virtual spots, higher proximal tubule program scores were associated with higher eGFR (partial r, 0.32) and less interstitial fibrosis (-0.57), and program-pathology associations agreed with those of measured Visium profiles in independent participants (Spearman rho, 0.64). Conclusions: Kidney-adapted virtual spatial transcriptomics links histology-derived molecular programs to experimental renal injury and human clinical and histologic phenotypes. Our approach enables spatial molecular analyses in routine biopsy histology, which could help decipher disease-associated pathways in existing biopsy archives.

papers.title: Fine-tuned encoders, generative large language models and typed decisions for classifying findings in chest CT reports: paired English-Japanese internal testing and external testing on naturally written Japanese reports
papers.abstract: Purpose: To compare fine-tuned encoders, generative large language models (LLMs) and typed decisions (per-finding yes/no questions answered with a probability) for classifying 18 findings in chest CT reports, and to identify when typed decisions help. Methods: This retrospective study used public data. The internal test set comprised 150 CT-RATE reports with paired Japanese translations at three quality levels; the external test set, 243 naturally written Japanese reports with human annotations (RR-Findings). We compared ModernBERT encoders fine-tuned on 20,444 reports, generative LLMs (gpt-6-luna, Qwen3.8-27B, MedGemma), and typed decisions with Jev, the Decisions API and Qwen. Thresholds fixed on 450 development reports were applied unchanged externally. The primary metric was micro-F1; case-level paired bootstrap 95% confidence intervals (CIs) were calculated for 11 internal comparisons. Results: Encoders were best internally (English 0.9853; radiologist-checked Japanese 0.9576) and exceeded Jev (differences 0.0367, 95% CI 0.0258-0.0484; 0.0336, 0.0215-0.0464). Externally, Jev (0.8844) lay within the encoder seed range (0.8656-0.9144), exceeded the three generative conditions tested externally (best 0.8564) and the Decisions API (0.8177), and had the smallest internal-to-external decrease (-0.0396). An encoder trained on 2,044 reports reached 0.8226 externally. Typed-versus-generated differences changed direction across models and test sets. At a fixed threshold of 0.5, Jev fell to 0.7753 externally. Conclusion: Fine-tuned encoders performed best with ample in-distribution labels. Although threshold-dependent, Jev, with thresholds fitted on only 450 labeled reports, fell within the encoder seed range externally and exceeded the generative LLMs and an encoder trained on 2,044 reports, making it an option when labels are scarce.

papers.title: Plasma Proteogenomic Uncovers Novel Molecular Mechanisms of Soluble Endoglin and Identifies AZI2 as a new Player in Arteriovenous Malformations in Hereditary Hemorrhagic Telangiectasia
papers.abstract: Endoglin is a transmembrane glycoprotein that plays a key role in vascular development, angiogenesis and endothelial homeostasis. Its soluble form (Sol-ENG), generated through proteolytic shedding of the membrane-bound protein, has been implicated in the pathophysiology of numerous cardiovascular diseases, ranging from common conditions such as preeclampsia and thrombosis to rare diseases such as hereditary hemorrhagic telangiectasia (HHT). Leveraging large-scale genomics, transcriptomics, proteomics and metabolomics data from public and original resources, we identify a molecular signature of 24 markers associated with plasma levels of Sol-ENG. This signature was enriched in genes coding for GPI-enchored proteins and included metabolites participating to glycosylation and redox homeostasis. Furthermore, we observed that ABO blood groups and genetically predicted plasma levels of 5-Azacytidine Induced 2 (AZI2) associate with the risk of arteriovenous malformations in HHT patients. This study provides new insights into the physiological mechanisms underlying Endoglin regulation and opens clinical perspectives for the management of HHT patients.

papers.title: Detection of Peanut Allergy Sensitization and Monitoring of Type 2 Memory B cells Using Recombinant Peanut Allergen Components
papers.abstract: Background Peanut allergy is one of the most common causes of life-threatening food allergy, and therefore the focus of multiple clinical trials for allergen immunotherapy. Diagnosis relies on detection of allergen-specific serum IgE, which provides limited information on severity and threshold. Furthermore, objective biomarkers to predict allergic persistence and efficacy of treatment are lacking. Therefore, we aimed to incorporate recombinant peanut allergen components in a multiplex Cytometric Basophil detection assay (CytoBas) for detection of peanut sensitization, and in a memory B cell (Bmem) panel for evaluation of biomarkers of disease. Methods In 27 adult peanut-allergic patients, allergen-specific IgE levels were determined by ImmunoCAP, and component-specific IgE by ELISA. PBMC of all patients and of 15 non-sensitized controls were analyzed by flow cytometry with basophil markers and six fluorochrome-conjugated allergen component tetramers for CytoBas, while circulating Bmem were studied including fluorescent tetramers for Ara h 1, Ara h 2 and Ara h 3. Results CytoBas demonstrated similar-to-improved diagnostic performance compared to IgE ELISAs for Ara h -1, -2, -3, -6, -8 allergens (ROCs AUC 0.79-1.0 versus 0.78-0.9). Ara h 2 discriminated all patients from controls, while combined Ara h 1, 3 and 6 (excluding major allergen Ara h 2) elicited 78-81% sensitivity with 100% specificity. Peanut-allergic patients showed expansion of the pathogenic Type 2 Bmem subset within Ara h 1-, 2- and 3-specific cells, and the Ara h 1+ and Ara h 3+ Bmem contained expanded IgG4+ and IgG1 subsets. Conclusions Peanut CytoBas displays similar to superior diagnostic accuracy to component-specific IgE serology, enabling efficient evaluation of multiple allergen components in a single test tube. Peanut-allergic individuals show increased frequencies of allergen-specific type 2 Bmem, which could be longitudinally evaluated to monitor the natural course of disease or allergen immunotherapy.

papers.title: A report-supervised EEG-language foundation model enables broad, interactive clinical interpretation
papers.abstract: Medical AI for complex signals such as electroencephalography (EEG) relies on costly expert annotations and predefined diagnostic labels that fail to capture the richness and nuance of clinical interpretation. Whether models trained on routine clinical reports can overcome these limitations while matching expert-supervised performance remains unclear. We introduce EEG Copilot, a biosignal-language foundation model trained on routine EEG-report pairs without dedicated task-specific expert annotations. Across two external datasets (6,078 EEGs), EEG Copilot performed on par with a state-of-the-art expert-supervised model across 11 shared findings (mean AUROC 0.80-0.81), corroborated by direct neurologist review of 200 EEGs. Beyond predefined diagnostic categories in conventional EEG AI, EEG Copilot assessed 23 clinical characteristics through natural-language questions in English and German across 9,689 EEGs from four hospitals (mean AUROC 0.80-0.82), demonstrating that automated EEG assessment need no longer be confined to fixed diagnostic outputs. Crucially, EEG Copilot generated integrated clinical impressions directly from EEG rather than isolated predictions with shuffled-report controls supporting recording-specific content and neurologist review of 800 impressions showing that most were accurate or clinically usable with minor errors. These findings chart a path beyond label-bound medical AI, transforming routine clinical reports into scalable supervision for flexible, language-driven assessment and integrated interpretation of complex physiological signals.

papers.title: Exploring the genetic determinants of ALS in a North Indian cohort using a genomic screening approach
papers.abstract: Background: Amyotrophic lateral sclerosis is a clinically and genetically heterogenous neurodegenerative disorder in which both monogenic and complex genetic mechanism contribute to disease susceptibility. Increasing evidence also indicates that non motor manifestations, including sleep disturbances, significantly influence disease burden. This study aimed to characterize the genetic spectrum of ALS in a predominantly North Indian cohort while evaluating the prevalence of sleep related abnormalities. Methods: Seventy-three clinically diagnosed ALS patients were recruited from a tertiary care centre in North India. Disease severity was assessed using the ALSFRS-R. Sleep quality, daytime sleepiness, and REM sleep behaviour disorder symptoms were evaluated using the PSQI, ESS and RBDQ questionnaires, respectively. Genetic analysis included targeted sequencing of SOD1, TARDBP, and ANG, followed by repeat expansion analysis of C9orf72, ATXN1, ATXN2, ATXN3, and ATXN7. Whole exome sequencing was performed in selected cases to further investigate the genetic basis of ALS. Results: The cohort demonstrated a male predominance and an earlier age of onset compared to many Western populations. Poor sleep quality and excessive daytime sleepiness were frequently observed although no significant association was found between sleep parameters and disease severity. Genetic screening identified a pathogenic/likely pathogenic TARDBP variant classified by ClinVar while no known or novel pathogenic variants were detected in SOD1 or ANG. Repeat expansion studies revealed one patient harbouring pathogenic C9orf72 repeat expansions. For the ATXN1, one patient harboured pathogenic repeat expansions and two patients carried intermediate length repeats. Additionally, one patient harboured intermediate repeat expansions in ATXN2. Whole exome sequencing revealed novel and rare variants in ALS associated genes including ANXA11, SIGMAR1, SETX, ERBB4 and NEK1, highlighting substantial genetic heterogeneity. Conclusions: Our findings highlight the complex genetic heterogeneity of ALS, with pathogenic repeat expansions and rare variants identified across multiple disease associated genes. These results demonstrate the importance of comprehensive genetic testing to improve the detection of clinically relevant variants in ALS. In addition, the high prevalence of sleep related disturbances observed in the cohort emphasizes the need to incorporate non motor assessment into routine clinical evaluation of patients with ALS.
